zh:
太白有诗云：海客谈瀛洲，烟涛微茫信难求。海客者，浮海之人也。钱塘当江海之会，番舶辐辏，遂有此巷，专聚四方商旅。
巷不甚长，而百货骈集。巷中所陈，多非中土所有——波斯之珠、大食之香、占城之沉、日南之翠，杂然并陈。至其人，则碧眼者、深目者、虬须者、文身者，无所不有。或裹首如塔，或袒臂佩环，操侏离之语，鬻诡谲之货，摩肩接踵，竟日喧阗。若言语不通，乃以手指物，屈指计数，亦能成市，亦一奇也。
客中亦有不复去者。久居既惯，渐染吴音，遂于巷侧赁屋市地，葺为小院。庭栽芭蕉，壁悬异锦，朝啜茗碗，暮饮蒲萄，俨然以钱塘为乡矣。问其故园，曰：风涛万里，归亦无期，何如老死此间。
胡马依北风，越鸟巢南枝。白乐天诗云：我生本无乡，心安是归处。彼海客者，非忘其乡也。以心之所安，即为乡耳。
en:
The poet Li Bai once wrote that seafarers tell of Yingzhou, a mythical isle lost in mist and crashing waves, impossible to find. As the Qiantang River meets the sea, it became a magnet for exactly these kinds of maritime voyagers. The convergence of foreign merchant fleets gave rise to a bustling alleyway dedicated entirely to hosting traders and travelers from the edge of the known world.
The alley itself isn't long, but it is practically bursting with commerce. You can find treasures here that are completely unknown in the Central Plains: Persian pearls, Arabian spices, Champa agarwood, and Rinan jade, all piled together in magnificent disarray. The crowds are just as dazzling. You pass men with piercing blue eyes and deep-set features, others with thick, curly beards or intricate tattoos. Some wear towering turbans, while others walk bare-armed, heavy with bangles. Shouting in incomprehensible languages, they hawk bizarre, exotic wares from dawn to dusk in the packed, noisy street. Amazingly, despite the language barrier, massive deals are struck every day simply by pointing at goods and flashing fingers to haggle.
Some of these merchants eventually decide to stay for good. As the years pass, they fall into the local rhythms, even picking up the lyrical lilt of the regional Wu dialect. They buy land along the alleyway and build homes with quiet courtyards. They plant native plantain trees in their gardens but hang exotic tapestries on their walls. Sipping local tea in the mornings and imported grape wine at night, they have essentially made Qiantang their new homeland. Ask them why, and they will tell you: "Our native lands are tens of thousands of miles away. The voyage back is at the mercy of fierce winds and killer waves, and you are never guaranteed to survive it. We might as well grow old and lay our bones to rest here."
An ancient proverb says that northern horses always lean into the north wind, and southern birds always build their nests on southward-facing branches. Yet, as the poet Bai Juyi once wrote: "I was born without a fixed homeland. Wherever my heart finds peace, that is my home." These seafarers haven't forgotten where they came from. They simply understand that home is wherever the heart can finally rest.
Yun Dan Feng Zhi Qing

zh:
《齐民要术·饼法》中有这样的记载：“作‘水引’、‘餄飥’，须用‘漏床’。床，以桑、槐之木为之，阔一尺，长二尺，孔如箸大。……以脚踏之，于沸汤上，做‘水引’、‘餄飥’。‘餄飥’，挼如大指许，长五寸。‘水引’，挼如箸大，长尺余。并皆揉润，截断，著床孔中，以脚踏之，使郎、郎然下，汤中寻索，即熟。”
到了宋朝，饸饹面已经成为了日常市井售卖的食物，如《东京梦华录》记载，“出朱雀门，直至龙津桥。……夏月，……并卖麻饮、细粉……盘合、河漏、……之类。”
en:
As recorded in the "Essential Techniques for the Welfare of the People": "To make 'water-drawn' noodles and 'Hele' noodles, a 'press bed' is required. The bed is made from mulberry or pagoda tree wood, one chi wide, two chi long, with holes the size of chopsticks... Using the foot to press on it over boiling water, 'Water-Drawn' and 'Hele' noodles are made. 'Hele' noodles are kneaded to the size of a thumb, about five cun long. 'Water-Drawn' noodles are kneaded to the thickness of chopsticks, over one chi long. Both are kneaded until pliable, cut, placed into the holes of the bed, and pressed with the foot, causing them to fall into the water. Sought in the broth, they are done in a moment."
By the Song Dynasty, Hele noodles had become common street food. As "A Dream of Splendor" notes: "Exit the Vermilion Bird Gate, straight to Longjin Bridge... In summer... also sold are 'ma drink', fine vermicelli... packaged meals, heluo (Hele) noodles, and the like."

zh: 县衙里有一只不知何时安家于此的灰狗。此狗没什么志向，每日就趴在院子里，有太阳就晒太阳，没太阳也没关系，反正都不影响它睡觉。大抵是来往于此处的小吏亦是无所事事，见着这狗总在院中呼呼大睡，于是谁路过都要伸手摸上一把。时间一久，狗头都被盘得油光发亮了。狗和人一样无事可做，只有肚子饿得咕咕叫的时候，才会懒懒地起身随便寻觅点吃食。若是恰好有人路过，就摇着尾巴靠近汪汪几声，圆溜溜的眼睛里透着几分讨好。长此以往，大家看透了这只小狗的殷勤，于是都管它叫咕咕了。咕咕喜欢人给它取的名字，因为每每有人这样唤它，它总能得到些零嘴甜头。直至某天杭州城落了场大雨，咕咕被淋成一只落汤狗，大家才恍然大悟：“哦哟！原来咕咕是只白狗儿呀！”
en: There is a gray dog at the county court, and no one remembers when he moved in. The dog has no ambitions to speak of. He sprawls out in the yard all day, basking in the sun when there is sun, and when there isn't, no matter, for it never troubles his sleep. It seems the minor clerks who come and go about the place have little to do either, and whenever they see the dog snoring in the yard, not one of them could resist reaching down for a pat. In time, the dog's head has been rubbed to a shine. The dog, much like the men, has nothing much to do, and only when his belly begins to rumble does he get up lazily to find something to eat. If someone happens to pass by, he wags his tail, trots over, and barks a few times, his round eyes gleaming with a touch of flattery. Before long, everyone has seen through the little dog's ways, and so they take to calling him Rumbles. Rumbles likes the name, for every time someone calls him that, a treat always follows. It was not until one day, when a heavy rain came down over Hangzhou and Rumbles was soaked to the skin, that everyone finally realized: "Oh my! Turns out Rumbles is a white dog!"

【桂花】

en:
【Hundred Flowers · Three】

【Osmanthus】

Ode to the Osmanthus
Li Bai
People plant peach and plum trees, all within the gates of the wealthy.
They scramble for shortcuts, vying for favor in the warm spring breeze.
But once the frost descends from heaven, their glory cannot long endure.
Who knows of the osmanthus on South Mountain, with green leaves and fragrant roots?
Its cool shade offers a place to rest; why begrudge planting it in your garden?

Gazing at the Moon on the Fifteenth Night, Sent to Attendant Du
Wang Jian
The courtyard ground is white, crows roost in trees,
Cold dew silently dampens the osmanthus flowers.
Tonight, all gaze at the bright moon,
But whose home does autumn longing fall upon?

【Chrysanthemum】

Chrysanthemums
Yuan Zhen
Autumn clusters surround my hut like Tao's home,
Circling the fence as the sun gradually slants.
It's not that among flowers I favor the chrysanthemum alone,
But when this flower blooms, no other remains.

Chrysanthemum
Li Shangyin
Dim, pale purple; warm, radiant yellow.
The colors by Tao's fence, the fragrance in Luo's hall.
How long can it withstand the heavy dew?
Truly it fears the waning sun.
I wish to float on a golden parrot cup,
And ascend to your white jade hall.

Ode to the Chrysanthemum After Failing the Imperial Exam
Huang Chao
Wait until autumn comes, the eighth day of the ninth month,
When my flower blooms, all other flowers perish.
Their soaring fragrance permeates Chang'an,
The entire city clad in golden armor.

【Orchid】

Twelve Feelings Encountered · One
Zhang Jiuling
Orchid leaves flourish in spring, osmanthus blooms bright in autumn.
Vigorous and full of life, each season brings its own beauty.
Who would have thought the forest dweller,
Hearing the wind, would sit and delight in them?
Grass and trees have their own nature,
Why seek for a beauty to pluck them?

Ode to the Orchid
Chen Ziang
Orchids grow in spring and summer, lush and verdant.
Solitary, they grace the empty woods, crimson blooms adorn purple stems.
The white day lingers, a gentle autumn breeze arises.
Years pass, all things wither and fall; what becomes of their fragrant intent?

【Pomegranate Flower】

Newly Planted Sea Pomegranate
Liu Zongyuan
A frail plant not a foot tall, its distant intent rests on Penglai.
Cold moon, empty steps at dawn, a hidden dream of colored clouds born.
From manure soil sprouts a pearl tree, amidst moss inserts a jade blossom.
Fragrant roots conceal their hue; for whom do they glory as years pass?

Sea Pomegranate
Wen Tingyun
Sea pomegranate red as fire, first to herald the spring wind.
Leaves, chaotically cut, are green as paper; flowers, best suited, adorn the hair in red.
Wax pearls cluster to form a stem, light silk cut into a bouquet.
At Zheng's post station, many thoughts of return; we meet with a shared smile.
Le Shui Li

安一飞翻着书页，指尖滑过一句“野马也，尘埃也，生物之以息相吹也”，得道高猫冷不丁喵了一声，安一飞纳罕地奉上书页：“你要叫哪个？息吹？”
不防得道高猫一个转身，猫屁股正对着安一飞，呛得女子一个踉跄，气恼拍案：“什么得道高猫，以后你就叫纵气！”
纵气轻盈一跃，尾巴在空中划过一道自在的弧线。
御气乘风是气，纵气放屁也是气，气嘛，本无高低雅俗。
只有聚散而已。
en:
The silver-tabby sat upright, its tail curled beneath like a tranquil meditation cushion. Amid a chaotic crowd of cats, it remained calm and composed—like a feline sage who had reached enlightenment. 
When An's fingertip paused on the line: "All beings share one breath," the so‑called enlightened cat meowed. She held the page out to it. "What, you want to be called 'Breath'?" 
Suddenly, the sage turned—and presented its rear without a hint of ceremony. The unexpected whiff sent her stumbling back. "From now on, you're called... 'Zong Qi'—'Unleashed Breath'!" 
With a graceful leap, Zong Qi soared, its tail tracing a carefree arc in the air. 
To ride the wind is qi; to break wind is qi as well. Qi carries no rank or refinement— 
it simply gathers, then scatters.

#Y联赛#E：周六、日晚8点半（百肆所在时区）进行，每个赛季联赛共有三个阶段：
#G筹备期（持续一周）#E：所有百业进行重新分组。
#G定级赛（持续三周）#E：每周六、日晚8点半（百肆所在时区）进行比赛，定级赛结束时根据战绩分配至逗圣、逗神、逗侠、暗逗四个组别。
#G常规赛（持续八周，每轮两周）#E：组别内进行比赛，每轮组内前4名升级，后4名降级。

#Y匹配赛#E：百业管理及指挥可匹配，每周六、日晚8点半到11点（百肆所在时区）可进行匹配。参与联赛的百业需在当天联赛结束后才能参与匹配赛。
每场比赛，每方百业最多#Y30名#E游侠可参与，游侠每天只能代表#Y一个#E百业参与百业战。
en:
Guild War has two modes: #YLeague#E and #YRanked Match#E. 

#YLeague#E: Held Saturdays and Sundays at 20:30 (in the Battlegroup's time zone). Each season consists of three phases: 
#GPrep Phase (1 week)#E: All Guilds are regrouped. 
#GPlacement Matches (3 weeks)#E: Held every Saturday and Sunday at 20:30 (in the Battlegroup's time zone). Guilds are assigned to Jesting Sage, Jesting God, Jesting Hero, or Stealth Jester groups based on results. 
#GRegular Season (8 weeks, 2 weeks per round)#E: Intra-group matches. Top 4 promote, bottom 4 demote each round. 

#YRanked Match#E: Available to Guild Admin Commanders on Saturdays and Sundays from 20:30 to 23:00 (in the Battlegroup's time zone). League participants can only join Ranked Match after their League match ends. 
Max #Y30#E Wanderers per Guild per match. Wanderers can only represent #Yone#E Guild in Guild War per day.

zh: 《春秋左传》成于战国初年，左丘明作。春秋三传之一，《春秋》经传初各单行，后人割传附经，遂成今本。本书以鲁国十二公为序，起鲁隐公元年，迄鲁哀公二十七年，多出《春秋》经文十三年。其文以叙事见长，详记列国聘问、会盟、征伐、篡弑、婚丧、祭祀诸事，兼及朝章典制、人物言行、鬼神灾异。其书常借“君子曰”发论，以明褒贬劝惩之义，又叙事详赡，脉络分明，既为解经之津梁，亦为史家之龟鉴。西汉初张苍、贾谊等传授其学，后尹更始、刘歆诸儒相继研治，章句之学渐兴。东汉贾逵、服虔等为之作注，郑玄亦有注《左传》未成。西晋杜预作《春秋经传集解》，合经传而注之。唐孔颖达奉诏修《春秋左传正义》，定为官学取士之本。
en: Zuo Zhuan, meaning "The Commentary of Zuo," was completed in the early Warring States period, composed by Zuo Qiuming. It is one of the Three Commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals. The canon and commentary originally circulated separately; later scholars divided the commentary and appended it to the canon, thus producing the text as it stands today. The work is arranged according to the sequence of the twelve lords of the state of Lu, beginning from the first year of Duke Yin of Lu and concluding at the twenty-seventh year of Duke Ai of Lu, extending thirteen years beyond the canon of the Spring and Autumn Annals itself. The work excels in narrative, recording in detail the diplomatic missions, covenant assemblies, military campaigns, usurpations and assassinations, marriages and funerals, and sacrificial rites of the various states, extending also to court regulations and canonical institutions, the words and conduct of characters, and matters of spirits, portents, and calamities. The text frequently employs the formula "the gentleman says" to advance its judgements, illuminating its righteousness of praise, censure, encouragement, and admonition. Its narrative is rich and thorough, its threads of reasoning clear, serving both as a bridge for the interpretation of the canon and as a mirror of warning for historians. In the early Western Han, Zhang Cang, Jia Yi, and others transmitted its learning; later, Yin Gengshi, Liu Xin, and successive scholars continued to study and elaborate upon it, and the tradition of chapter-and-verse scholarship gradually flourished. In the Eastern Han, Jia Kui, Fu Qian, and others composed annotations for it, and Zheng Xuan also began but did not complete an annotation of Zuo Zhuan. In the Western Jin, Du Yu composed the Collected Interpretations of the Spring and Autumn Canon and Commentary, annotating canon and commentary together. In the Tang, Kong Yingda received an imperial decree to compile the Correct Meaning of Zuo Zhuan on the Spring and Autumn Annals, establishing it as the foundation for the official examinations.

zh:
旄、节、旌、旗为中国古代礼仪制度中的重要仪仗标识。
节为君主行使特殊使命的凭信；旄是以牦牛尾为饰的长杆，旄节则在旄首下再串牛旄或羽旄，象征军事指挥权；旌为旄牛尾或兼五色鸟羽装饰竿头的旗子，而旌节是使臣所持的信物；旗以帛为面，用于等级标识和军事指挥。
随着礼制规范与实用需求的不断演变，几者的功能和形态有所交叉。为统一剧情传达，符合直观认知，十六巷以旄节为统称，来涵盖其作为信物、军权符号及身份象征等的多元意义。
en:
In ancient China, mao (banner tassels), jie (tally tokens), jing (ceremonial flags), and qi (flags) held great significance within the rituals of state. 
The jie was a royal token of authority, while the mao was a yak-tail-adorned pole; together as maojie, they symbolized military command. The jing were flags, and the qi were silk flags marking rank and directing armies. 
Over time, their distinctions blurred, and all were collectively called maojie, representing power, military command, and status.
Jiang Shaozhi丶

zh:
"臣与先帝识于微时。臣出身贫寒，空有凌云之志，却无伯乐之遇。济河求仕，亦因官场舞弊，屡考不中，流落街头几饿死。先帝大善，身上唯余一粗饼，却愿予臣分食。臣远赴洛阳，是为辅佐明君，然何谓明君？隐帝正统，却无治世之才。刘知远有勇，却骄奢贪婪。郭威执掌兵权，行事却谨小慎微，其二子更是庸碌之辈！唯有先帝，不以臣失意而轻之，心怀天下，智勇双全。先帝在位时，天下太平，实为臣之幸也。

惜哉！先帝崩后，臣几欲涕零，然思及赵匡胤虎视眈眈，小公子亦尚且年幼，臣需当之。一饭之恩应永铭于心，然赏识之重当万世报还。"

——《魏仁浦手书》
en:
"I first met the Late Emperor in the days of my obscurity. Born into poverty, I bared grand ambitions yet found no patron to recognize my worth. I crossed the river seeking office, but corruption riddled the bureaucracy, causing me to fail the examinations time and again, I nearly perished destitute on the streets. The Late Emperor, magnanimous beyond measure, though possessing nothing more than a coarse cake, shared it with me without hesitation. Thus, I journeyed to Luoyang to aid a true sovereign, but what is a true sovereign? Emperor Yin held rightful claim yet lacked the talent to govern; Liu Zhiyuan was bold, but arrogant and greedy; Guo Wei commanded the armies but was overly cautious, and his sons were naught but mediocrities. Only the Late Emperor, who never scorned me for my failures, held the world in his heart and was peerless in both wisdom and courage. During his reign, the realm remained peaceful. It was my greatest fortune to serve him.

Alas! After the Late Emperor's passing, I could scarcely hold back my tears. Yet with Zhao Kuangyin eyeing the throne and the young prince still but a child, I could not afford to weep. A single meal of kindness must be repaid with a lifetime of loyalty, much more so a debt as great as his favor and trust!"

—Handwritten Memoirs of Wei Renpu

【丧服小记第十五】

斩衰，括发以麻，为母括发以麻，免而以布。齐衰，恶笄以终丧。男子冠而妇人笄，男子免而妇人髽。其义：为男子则免，为妇人则髽。
苴杖，竹也；削杖，桐也。
祖父卒，而后为祖母后者三年。
为父母，长子稽颡。大夫吊之，虽缌必稽颡。妇人为夫与长子稽颡，其余则否。
男主必使同姓，妇主必使异姓。
为父后者，为出母无服。
亲亲以三为五，以五为九，上杀、下杀、旁杀，而亲毕矣。
王者禘其祖之所自出，以其祖配之，而立四庙。庶子王亦如之。
别子为祖，继别为宗，继祢者为小宗。有五世而迁之宗，其继高祖者也。是故祖迁于上，宗易于下。尊祖故敬宗，敬宗所以尊祖祢也。
庶子不祭祖者，明其宗也。庶子不为长子斩，不继祖与祢故也。庶子不祭殇与无后者，殇与无后者从祖祔食。
庶子不祭祢者，明其宗也。
……
en:
【Mourning Garments and Minor Records, Chapter 15】

For the mourning of a father, the hair is bound with hemp; for the mourning of a mother, the hair is also bound with hemp, but after the ritual of removal, a cloth band is used. For the mourning of one year (Qi Cui), the mourning pin of a coarse hairpin is worn until the end of the mourning period. Men wear the cap, and women wear the hairpin; men perform the ritual of removal (Mian), and women wear the mourning coiffure (Zhua). The principle is: for men, the Mian is used; for women, the Zhua is used.
The unadorned staff is made of bamboo; the trimmed staff is made of tung wood.
When the grandfather has died, and one becomes the heir of the grandmother, the mourning lasts three years.
For the death of parents, the eldest son knocks his head on the ground (Qisang). When a high official comes to offer condolences, even if the mourning is for a distant relative (Si), one must perform the Qisang. Women perform the Qisang for their husbands and eldest sons; for others, they do not.
The male host must be of the same surname, and the female host must be of a different surname.
For one who is the heir of the father, there is no mourning for a divorced mother.
The affection for relatives extends from three to five, and from five to nine; it diminishes upward, downward, and laterally, and then the kinship is complete.
A king performs the Di sacrifice to his ancestor's origin, matching him with his ancestor, and establishes four ancestral temples. Even a son of a concubine who becomes king does the same.
The separate son becomes the ancestor; those who continue the separate line form the main lineage; those who continue the line of the deceased father form the minor lineage. There are lineages that are moved after five generations; these are those that continue the line of the great-great-grandfather. Therefore, when the ancestor is moved above, the lineage changes below. Respecting the ancestor, one honors the lineage head; honoring the lineage head is the way to respect the ancestor and the father.
The son of a concubine does not sacrifice to the ancestor, to clarify the lineage. The son of a concubine does not wear the three-year mourning for the eldest son, because he does not continue the line of the ancestor and the father. The son of a concubine does not sacrifice to those who died young or those without heirs, for those who died young and those without heirs are fed together with the ancestor in the ancestral temple.
The son of a concubine does not sacrifice to the deceased father, to clarify the lineage.
……

Those further away killed in a month or two, and farthest could remain lethal for up to one to three years. Only the Chen family's antidotes offered a cure.

zh:
“破茧而出的飞蛾，还是结茧时的那只蚕吗？”
很久以前孩子这样问过他。徐文清——那时候他还叫徐永，一时给不出回答。直到经由春蚕之术脱胎换骨，他才觉得心中有了定论：当然是。它们有相同的魂灵。
但那具被他抛下的“死蛾”，似乎并不这么想。

夜半惊醒，提刀摸进他房中的人额头生着怪异的突触——他认出那是他自己家的护卫。此刻在暗夜中狂奔，这具年轻的躯体显得如此轻盈，不像衰老时迈出的每一步都那么吃力。衰老的感觉是迟滞的、黏稠的，因为嚼不烂食物，连吞咽都需要花大力气，令人羞愧。那是属于老徐永的记忆，即使改头换面，那无力感如影随形，连在逃命时都要扒上来。他甩了甩头。眼下顾不得这些了。这具千辛万苦换来的年轻肉身偏偏孱弱得毫无还手之力。最要紧的是逃命，逃出去，逃出他自己的山庄。
已被惨叫与嘶吼淹没的山庄。
但很快，他突然意识到了一件事。逃离的脚步骤然停下。
血。
下一次饮血的十日大限快到了。逃出山庄一样是死。
唯一的庆幸，是这具少年的身体足够瘦小。最后，他找到了办法。

马明王庙的祈蚕会明日就要开场了。只要有人能替他闯进山庄，引开这群叛徒虫奴，他就有机会趁乱溜回地下神床，偷到一点续命的血。陈旧的，发臭的，原本属于他自己的血。
庄园里的惨叫声渐渐弱了。风声簌簌，西湖的春水正一下下拍打着山庄的石堤。雀鸟开始啼鸣。天应该快亮了。
他在狭小的贡品箱里蜷紧身体，如同又做一回缩在茧里的春蚕。
木茧里一片漆黑。他想象着西湖的日出，闭上眼睛。
en:
"Is a moth that has broken free of its cocoon still the same silkworm that once spun it?"
A child once asked him that, long ago. Xu Wenqing, who still went by Xu Yong then, had no answer for it. Only after the Spring Silkworm Technique remade him did he find the answer: Of course it is. They share the same soul.
But the "dead moth" he cast aside seemed to disagree.

He woke with a start at night to someone creeping into his room with a blade. The man had strange growths sprouting from his brow—he recognized him as one of his own guards. Now, fleeing through the dark, this young body felt so light. Nothing like the old days, when every step was labored. Old age was sluggish, viscous. He couldn't chew his food properly, and even swallowing took an effort that shamed him. Those were old Xu Yong's memories, and even with a new face, that helplessness clung to him like a shadow, dragging at him even as he ran for his life. He shook his head. No time to dwell on such things now. This young flesh, won at such cost, was frustratingly frail, unable to fight back. All that mattered was getting out, out of his own villa.
A villa already drowned in screams and howls.
Then something struck him, and he stopped dead.
Blood.
The ten days were nearly up, and he had to drink again. Fleeing the villa meant death all the same.
Thankfully, this youth's body was small and thin. His one stroke of fortune. In the end, he found a way.

The Silkworm Prayer Assembly at Hayagriva Temple would begin tomorrow. If only someone could break into the villa in his stead and draw away those traitor worm-servants, he could slip back to the underground Divine Repose amid the chaos and steal a little blood to keep going. Old, foul blood. Blood that had once been his own.
The screams within the estate were fading. The wind rustled, and the spring waters of West Lake lapped against the villa's stone embankment. Birds began to sing. Dawn must be near.
He curled up tight within the cramped tribute chest, a spring silkworm coiled inside its cocoon once more.
The wooden cocoon was pitch dark. He pictured the sunrise over West Lake, and closed his eyes.

zh:
很久以前，慧药还是个小和尚。
那时候，落发为僧是件稀松平常的事，做和尚有饭吃，仅此而已，无关信仰。
他就念着半生不熟的经，在慈心山院做一天和尚，撞一天钟。

直到后来，那个叫妙善的禅师来了，成了他的师父。
慧药第一次觉得，世上原来真有佛陀。
世上竟真有这样的人物，懂佛法渊博、有佛光神通、还救苦救难。
师父教他读经，教他佛祖舍身饲虎、普度众生，师父的佛光，似乎真的照进他心中。
他开始真的相信佛，相信自己被爱、众生被爱。他成了最虔诚的佛徒，早课晚课、焚香诵经，一日不落，他也如愿成了妙善门下的大弟子，常伴师父左右。

然后，他发现了师父的秘密。
原来这一场欺世之局里，他和众生，都被算计。
他脆弱的信仰尽数崩塌，随即接受了那种妖异的紫色花朵。

慧药暗暗地笑了。
善也好，恶也罢，慧药的一切，都由你传授……
师父，我们果然是天生注定的师徒。
en:
Long ago, Huiyao was just a young monk.
In those days, shaving one's head to become a monk was a mundane thing—simply a way to get fed, nothing to do with faith.
He mumbled half-remembered sutras, ringing the bell and going through the motions at Mercyheart Monastery day after day.

All that changed when Miaoshan arrived and became his teacher.
For the first time, Huiyao believed there might truly be a Buddha in this world.
How could someone like this exist? Profound in Buddhist teachings, endowed with divine light and supernatural powers, and dedicated to saving the suffering.
His master taught him to recite sutras, told him stories of the Buddha sacrificing himself to feed a tiger and delivering all sentient beings from suffering. It seemed the master's light of the Buddha had truly entered his heart.
He began to truly believe in Buddhism, to believe he was loved, that all beings were loved. He became the most devout disciple, never missing a morning or evening ritual, burning incense and chanting sutras without fail. As he wished, he became Miaoshan's principal disciple, always by the master's side.

Then he discovered his master's secret. It turned out that in this entire deceptive scheme, he and all living beings had been manipulated. 
His fragile faith collapsed entirely, and he accepted those strange purple flowers.

Huiyao smiled faintly.
Good or evil, everything I am, you have taught me...
Master, we are indeed fated to be master and disciple.
Unbowed, Unbroken

zh:
采桑子，词牌名，又称《罗敷媚》、《丑奴儿》等。双调四十四字，上下阕各四句、三平韵，一韵到底。上下阕第三句常用叠韵。采桑子源于唐代教坊曲《杨下采桑》。南唐李煜词名《丑奴儿令》，冯延巳词名《罗敷媚歌》，贺铸词名《丑奴儿》，陈师道词名《罗敷媚》。
现存谱子见于日本《博雅笛谱》。
en: Mulberry Picker is the title of a classic Ci-poem melody pattern, also known by names such as Luofu's Charm and Little Rascal. It features a double-tone structure of forty-four characters, with both the upper and lower stanzas comprising four lines each. It maintains a single level-tone rhyme scheme throughout, and the third line of both stanzas frequently employs repeating syllables. The melody originated from a Tang dynasty royal conservatory piece titled Picking Mulberries Beneath the Poplar. Various poets favored it, giving it distinct names: Li Yu of the Southern Tang called it Song of the Little Rascal, Feng Yansi named it Song of Luofu's Charm, while He Zhu and Chen Shidao also adopted these alternate titles. Its surviving musical score can be found in the Japanese compilation Boya Flute Score.

en: Though the Inkbound Order holds many duties to be attended—guarding, patrol, and the keeping of provisions among them—no servants are hired; all such tasks fall to the students themselves. Save for the Printing Workshop, the Paper Mill, and the kitchens of the Dining Hall, which demand specialized skill and cannot be entrusted to the untrained, all other duties—sweeping the Dining Hall, airing books in the courtyard, distributing sundry goods, and tending to the Study Hall—are shared among the students by rotation, with each month's assignments decided by draws. Beyond this, the Order treats all students alike without distinction; regardless of birth or station, rich or poor, each must see to their own daily needs: their rising and resting, their washing and laundering. Thus the students of the Inkbound Order are not merely learned in letters and principle. They know also the weight of toil, and the bonds between fellow scholars are, through shared labor, all the deeper for it.

zh:
【商书·汤誓】

伊尹相汤伐桀，升自陑，遂与桀战于鸣条之野，作《汤誓》。
王曰：“格尔众庶，悉听朕言。非台小子敢行称乱！有夏多罪，天命殛之。今尔有众，汝曰：‘我后不恤我众，舍我穑事，而割正夏？’予惟闻汝众言，夏氏有罪，予畏上帝，不敢不正。今汝其曰：‘夏罪其如台？’夏王率遏众力，率割夏邑。有众率怠弗协，曰：‘时日曷丧？予及汝皆亡。’夏德若兹，今朕必往。尔尚辅予一人，致天之罚，予其大赉汝！尔无不信，朕不食言。尔不从誓言，予则孥戮汝，罔有攸赦。”
汤既胜夏，欲迁其社，不可。作夏社、疑至、臣扈。
夏师败绩，汤遂从之。遂伐三朡，俘厥宝玉。谊伯、仲伯作典宝。
en:
【Book of Shang · The Oath of Tang】

Yi Yin assisted Tang in punishing Jie, ascending from Er, and then fought against Jie in the wilderness of Mingtiao, composing the "Oath of Tang."
The king said: "Come, all you multitudes, listen carefully to my words. It is not that I, a mere man, dare to initiate rebellion! Xia has committed many crimes, and Heaven has decreed its destruction. Now, all of you, you say: 'Our ruler does not show compassion for our multitudes, but abandons our agricultural work to punish Xia?' I have heard your words, but the Xia clan has committed crimes. I fear the Supreme God and dare not refrain from punishing them. Now you may say: 'What harm has Xia actually done?' The Xia king has exhausted the strength of the people and has cruelly plundered the cities of Xia. The multitudes have become negligent and uncooperative, saying: 'When will this sun perish? We would rather perish together with you.' Such is the virtue of Xia. Now I must go. If you will assist me, one man, in executing Heaven's punishment, I will greatly reward you! Do not doubt me, for I will not break my word. If you do not obey this oath, I will make slaves of your wives and children, and there will be no pardon."
After Tang had defeated Xia, he wished to move their altar of the earth god, but found it inappropriate. He therefore composed the "Xia She," "Yi Zhi," and "Chen Hu."
The Xia army was utterly defeated, and Tang pursued them. He then attacked Sandong and captured their precious jade. Yi Bo and Zhong Bo composed the "Dian Bao."

可是每次见到赵大那朴实的样子，大家又忍不住怀疑起自个儿的想法来。像他这样的人，能是什么天潢贵胄？
en:
Mention Big Zhao anywhere in Kaifeng, and you'll hear nothing but praise. 

Though he wasn't often seen, those who did run into him were almost always in luck. Doesn't matter if you're close or just an acquaintance—if you've run into trouble and mention it to him, he'll go out of his way to pull strings and find someone who can help. Ask him how he pulled it off, and he just gives you a quiet smile. Eventually, the neighbors started spinning their own tales. Wild guesses about who he really was, where he came from, what kind of hidden background he might have. 

And yet, every time they saw him again, that plain, honest face always made them doubt their own imaginations. Could someone like him really be some high-born noble?

zh: 商城展示-战国袍-移动端-男

朱色，取个“工”字——像晚霞，像秋枫……中秋，合该食蟹！叹凉州无蟹……听长安来的商队说，中原秋蟹肥了，掰开壳能流出黄灿灿的膏，蘸醋吃——啧，等开春商队再来，定要托他们捎坛醋，就着这满墙“蟹蝥”下饭！嗯……阿弥陀佛，菩萨莫怪。
——蟹蝥红。

黄色，取“廿”字——杏子，葵花，栀子香……听说长安的栀子洁白无暇，香气又甜又怯，怕是耐不住凉州风雪。栀子花香，藏经洞里嗅不到，卧佛寺下见不着，可经书里却写了另一种栀子香——“薝蔔花”，西方净土孕育出的金黄圣花，清芳可爱，菩萨最是喜欢。只要做好事，行功德，菩萨笑眯了眼，天上便会降下花雨，众生闻香得度——既如此，不慎点上的这几抹黄，便算作了佛光花雨，想来菩萨大度，不会同我计较吧？
——栀子黄。

绿色，取“夕”字——玉门关外不见绿，凉州雪盛，苍郁难觅。这抹绿……像家前的绿柳，像塘里的荷叶，也像家后的那座碧山。小时候觉着山大，郁郁葱葱，进去了便要迷路，再回不了家。长大后才知晓，山虽大，却永远在家的后方。人就算不往山里去，也会迷路的。届时只要闭上眼，若能见山，家便不远了。
——碧山绿。

青色，取青字头——这颜色，我曾听见过。宿在佛寺的那一夜，风声呜咽，令人难以安眠。恍惚间，似有微弱笛音，自厢房外的竹林深处传来……若是循声而去，那花鸟精怪，不知能否听懂人言，让我画上一笔？若是不去，未免辜负良辰，佳人，知音……忽地笛声断了，话本子被吹落下案，窗外月正明。
——竹月青。

白色……这白不像凉州的雪，不像月下的沙，白垩摸起来细细滑滑……是不是有些像，寺里祈福的女眷说起过的，荔枝？她们说那果子生在岭南，剥开壳，里头是雪白透亮的肉，柔润晶莹……这抹白，用来画观音的指尖正好。咳，我可没有不敬之心，只是有些羡慕罢了……不过，要我指尖也这样好看了，那可就提不了笔了。
——荔肉白。
en:
This vermilion hue—it reminds me of the sunset glow, of autumn maples... Mid-Autumn is for feasting on crabs! Alas, in Liangzhou, there are no crabs to be found. Merchants from Chang'an speak of the autumn crabs of the Central Plains, plump and rich, their shells cracking open to reveal oozing, golden roe, best savored with a dip of vinegar... Tsk. When the caravans return in spring, I must ask them to bring a jar of vinegar. Then I can pair it with this wall of "crab roe" for my meal! Ahem... Amitabha, may the Bodhisattvas forgive my worldly thoughts.

—Crab Roe Red.

This shade of yellow—like apricots, sunflowers, the scent of gardenias... I hear the gardenias of Chang'an are flawless white, their fragrance sweet and shy—too delicate, I fear, to endure the wind and snow of Liangzhou. One cannot smell gardenias in the Sutra Caves, nor find them near the Reclining Buddha Temple. Yet the scriptures speak of another kind of gardenia fragrance—the Zhanbo flower, a sacred golden bloom from the Western Pure Land. It is pure and lovely, a favorite of the Bodhisattvas. They say if you perform good deeds and accumulate merit, the Bodhisattvas will smile, and a rain of fragrant flowers will fall from the heavens, guiding all beings to enlightenment with its scent. In that case, these few accidental smudges of yellow can be counted as the light of Buddha and a rain of sacred flowers. I imagine the Bodhisattvas are generous and will not hold it against me.
—Gardenia Yellow.

This shade of green... One sees no green beyond the Jade Gate Pass. In Liangzhou, the snows are heavy, and verdant life is hard to find. This splash of green... it's like the willow trees in front of my home, the lotus leaves in the pond, and the emerald mountain behind my house. As a child, the mountain seemed immense and lush, a place to get lost in and never return. Only after growing up did I understand that though the mountain is vast, it always stands behind home. One can get lost in life even without venturing into the mountains. In those moments, you need only close your eyes. If you can see the mountain, home is not far.
—Emerald Mountain Green.

This color, this cyan... I believe I have heard it before. That night I lodged at the monastery, the wind wailed, making sleep impossible. In a daze, I seemed to hear the faint sound of a flute, drifting from deep within the bamboo grove outside my room... If I had followed the sound, I wonder if the spirits of flowers and birds would have understood my words and let me capture their likeness with a single stroke? But to not go would be to waste a perfect moment, a beautiful presence, a kindred sound... Then, suddenly, the flute fell silent. A gust of wind blew my storybook from the desk. Outside, the moon was intensely bright.
—Moonlit Bamboo Cyan.

This white... it's not like the snow of Liangzhou, nor the sand under the moon. This chalk powder feels fine and smooth to the touch... Is it not a bit like what the devout ladies at the temple speak of—the lychee? They say the fruit grows in the southern lands. You peel back the shell to find flesh as white as snow and translucent, soft and glistening... This shade of white would be perfect for painting the fingertips of Guanyin. Ahem, I mean no disrespect, of course. It is only a bit of envy... Then again, if my own fingertips were so lovely, I would no longer be able to hold a brush.
—Lychee Flesh White.
Xiahou Ning Jin

zh:
【上经·䷀】

䷀
乾：元，亨，利，贞。
初九，潜龙勿用。
九二，见龙在田，利见大人。
九三，君子终日乾乾，夕惕若厉，无咎。
九四，或跃在渊，无咎。
九五，飞龙在天，利见大人。
上九，亢龙有悔。
用九，见群龙无首，吉。
《彖》曰：大哉乾元！万物资始，乃统天。云行雨施，品物流形。大明终始，六位时成，时乘六龙以御天。乾道变化，各正性命，保合大和，乃利贞。首出庶物，万国咸宁。
《象》曰：天行健，君子以自强不息。“潜龙勿用”，阳在下也；“见龙在田”，德施普也；“终日乾乾”，反复道也；“或跃在渊”，进无咎也；“飞龙在天”，大人造也；“亢龙有悔”，盈不可久也；“用九”，天德不可为首也。
《文言》曰：元者，善之长也；亨者，嘉之会也；利者，义之和也；贞者，事之干也。君子体仁足以长人，嘉会足以合礼，利物足以和义，贞固足以干事。君子行此四德者，故曰：“乾：元，亨，利，贞。”
初九曰“潜龙勿用”，何谓也？子曰：“龙德而隐者也。不易乎世，不成乎名；遁世无闷，不见是而无闷；乐则行之，忧则违之，确乎其不可拔，‘潜龙’也。”
九二曰“见龙在田，利见大人”，何谓也？子曰：“龙德而正中者也。庸言之信，庸行之谨；闲邪存其诚，善世而不伐，德博而化。《易》曰：‘见龙在田，利见大人’，君德也。”
九三曰“君子终日乾乾，夕惕若厉，无咎”，何谓也？子曰：“君子进德修业。忠信，所以进德也；修辞立其诚，所以居业也。知至至之，可与几也；知终终之，可与存义也。是故居上位而不骄，在下位而不忧。故乾乾因其时而惕，虽危无咎矣。”
九四曰“或跃在渊，无咎”，何谓也？子曰：“上下无常，非为邪也；进退无恒，非离群也。君子进德修业，欲及时也，故‘无咎’。”
九五曰“飞龙在天，利见大人”，何谓也？子曰：“同声相应，同气相求；水流湿，火就燥；云从龙，风从虎；圣人作而万物睹；本乎天者亲上，本乎地者亲下，则各从其类也。”
上九曰“亢龙有悔”，何谓也？子曰：“贵而无位，高而无民，贤人在下位而无辅，是以动而‘有悔’也。”
“潜龙勿用”，下也；“见龙在田”，时舍也；“终日乾乾”，行事也；“或跃在渊”，自试也；“飞龙在天”，上治也；“亢龙有悔”，穷之灾也；乾元“用九”，天下治也。
“潜龙勿用”，阳气潜藏；“见龙在田”，天下文明；“终日乾乾”，与时偕行；“或跃在渊”，乾道乃革；“飞龙在天”，乃位乎天德；“亢龙有悔”，与时偕极；乾元“用九”，乃见天则。
“乾，元”者，始而亨者也；“利，贞”者，性情也。乾始能以美利利天下，不言所利，大矣哉！大哉乾乎，刚健中正，纯粹精也；六爻发挥，旁通情也；时乘六龙，以御天也；云行雨施，天下平也。
君子以成德为行，日可见之行也。“潜”之为言也，隐而未见，行而未成，是以君子弗用也。
君子学以聚之，问以辩之，宽以居之，仁以行之。《易》曰“见龙在田，利见大人”，君德也。
九三重刚而不中，上不在天，下不在田，故乾乾因其时而惕，虽危无咎矣。
九四重刚而不中，上不在天，下不在田，中不在人，故“或”之。“或”之者，疑之也，故无咎。
夫“大人”者，与天地合其德，与日月合其明，与四时合其序，与鬼神合其吉凶。先天而天弗违，后天而奉天时。天且弗违，而况于人乎？况于鬼神乎？
“亢”之为言也，知进而不知退，知存而不知亡，知得而不知丧。其唯圣人乎，知进退存亡，而不失其正者，其唯圣人乎！
en:
【Upper Canon · Hexagram 1 ☰】

☰
Qian: Prime, Prosperous, Beneficial, and Persevering.
Initial Nine: The hidden dragon does not act.
Nine in the Second: The dragon appears in the field; it is beneficial to see the great person.
Nine in the Third: The noble man is vigorous and diligent all day; in the evening he remains vigilant, as if in danger—no blame.
Nine in the Fourth: He may leap in the deep; no blame.
Nine in the Fifth: The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is beneficial to see the great person.
Top Nine: The proud dragon will have regret.
Using Nine: See the flock of dragons without heads—auspicious.
The Tuan Commentary says: Great indeed is the Prime Essence of Qian! All things owe their beginning to it, and it unifies the heavens. Clouds move and rain falls; all things flow into their forms. The Great Light reaches its end and beginning; the six positions are accomplished in their time, riding the six dragons at the proper moment to govern the heavens. The Dao of Qian transforms, and each thing attains its correct nature and destiny; preserving the great harmony brings what is beneficial and persevering. It leads forth all beings, and all nations enjoy peace.
The Xiang Commentary says: Heaven's vigor moves ceaselessly; the noble man strengthens himself without rest. "The hidden dragon does not act"—the yang is below; "The dragon appears in the field"—virtue spreads universally; "Vigorous and diligent all day"—he repeatedly practices the Dao; "He may leap in the deep"—advancing brings no blame; "The flying dragon is in the heavens"—the great person creates; "The proud dragon will have regret"—fullness cannot last long; "Using Nine"—the virtue of Heaven cannot take the lead.
The Wenyan Commentary says: "Prime" is the chief of goodness; "Prosperous" is the gathering of what is excellent; "Beneficial" is the harmony of righteousness; "Persevering" is the foundation of affairs. The noble man, embodying benevolence, is sufficient to lead others; gathering what is excellent is sufficient to accord with propriety; benefiting all things is sufficient to harmonize righteousness; being firm and persevering is sufficient to accomplish affairs. The noble man practices these four virtues, therefore it is said: "Qian: Prime, Prosperous, Beneficial, and Persevering."
Initial Nine says "The hidden dragon does not act"—what does this mean? The Master said: "This is one with dragon virtue who remains in seclusion. He is not swayed by the world, nor does he seek fame; he withdraws from the world without distress, and is not troubled when unrecognized. He delights in what he does and avoids what worries him; he is firm and cannot be uprooted—this is the 'hidden dragon.'"
Nine in the Second says "The dragon appears in the field; it is beneficial to see the great person"—what does this mean? The Master said: "This is one with dragon virtue who is correct and centered. His ordinary words are trustworthy, his ordinary conduct is careful; he guards against what is improper and preserves his sincerity, benefits the world without boasting, and his virtue is broad and transforming. The Yi says: 'The dragon appears in the field; it is beneficial to see the great person'—this is the virtue of a ruler."
Nine in the Third says "The noble man is vigorous and diligent all day; in the evening he remains vigilant, as if in danger—no blame"—what does this mean? The Master said: "The noble man advances in virtue and cultivates his work. Loyalty and trustworthiness are how he advances in virtue; refining his words and establishing his sincerity are how he dwells in his work. Knowing the goal, he reaches it—he can grasp the subtle beginnings; knowing the end, he completes it—he can preserve righteousness. Therefore, in a high position he is not arrogant, and in a low position he is not anxious. Thus he is vigorous and diligent, vigilant according to the time—though in danger, there is no blame."
Nine in the Fourth says "He may leap in the deep; no blame"—what does this mean? The Master said: "Going up and down without constancy is not for the sake of evil; advancing and retreating without fixed rule is not for abandoning the group. The noble man advances in virtue and cultivates his work, wishing to seize the moment—therefore there is 'no blame.'"
Nine in the Fifth says "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is beneficial to see the great person"—what does this mean? The Master said: "Like sounds respond to like sounds; like qi seeks like qi; water flows to what is wet, fire approaches what is dry; clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger; when the Emperor arises, all things behold him; those rooted in Heaven draw near to what is above, those rooted in Earth draw near to what is below—each follows its own kind."
Top Nine says "The proud dragon will have regret"—what does this mean? The Master said: "Noble but without position, high but without the people, worthy persons are below without assisting him—therefore when he acts, he 'has regret.'"
"The hidden dragon does not act"—he is below; "The dragon appears in the field"—the time has come to rest; "Vigorous and diligent all day"—he is conducting affairs; "He may leap in the deep"—he is testing himself; "The flying dragon is in the heavens"—he governs from above; "The proud dragon will have regret"—this is the calamity of exhaustion; the Prime Essence of Qian "uses Nine"—the world is governed.
"The hidden dragon does not act"—the yang qi is hidden and stored; "The dragon appears in the field"—the world is enlightened and civilized; "Vigorous and diligent all day"—he moves with the times; "He may leap in the deep"—the Dao of Qian is transformed; "The flying dragon is in the heavens"—he is positioned in the virtue of Heaven; "The proud dragon will have regret"—he reaches the extreme with the times; the Prime Essence of Qian "uses Nine"—thereupon the rule of Heaven is revealed.
"Qian, Prime"—it is the beginning that brings prosperity; "Beneficial, Persevering"—these are its nature and disposition. Qian in its beginning is able to benefit all under Heaven with beautiful benefits, yet it does not speak of what it benefits—how great it is! How great is Qian! Firm, strong, centered, and correct, pure and refined in essence; the six lines unfold and penetrate all emotions; riding the six dragons at the proper time to govern the heavens; clouds move and rain falls—all under Heaven is at peace.
The noble man takes the completion of virtue as his conduct, visible in his daily actions. The word "hidden" means concealed and not yet seen, acting but not yet accomplished—therefore the noble man does not employ it.
The noble man learns to accumulate, questions to discern, dwells broadly, and acts with benevolence. The Yi says "The dragon appears in the field; it is beneficial to see the great person"—this is the virtue of a ruler.
Nine in the Third is doubled firmness yet not centered; above, it is not in Heaven; below, it is not in the field—therefore he is vigorous and diligent, vigilant according to the time—though in danger, there is no blame.
Nine in the Fourth is doubled firmness yet not centered; above, it is not in Heaven; below, it is not in the field; in the middle, it is not among humans—therefore it says "perhaps." "Perhaps" means doubt—therefore there is no blame.
As for the "great person": his virtue accords with Heaven and Earth; his brightness accords with the sun and moon; his order accords with the four seasons; his auspiciousness and inauspiciousness accord with the ghosts and spirits. Going before Heaven, Heaven does not oppose him; following Heaven, he serves the time of Heaven. Heaven itself does not oppose him—how much less humans? How much less ghosts and spirits?
The word "proud" means knowing how to advance but not how to retreat, knowing how to preserve but not how to perish, knowing how to gain but not how to lose. Is this not only the Emperor? One who knows advance and retreat, preservation and perishing, without losing his correctness—is this not only the Emperor?

zh:
【冬官考工记第六】

国有六职，百工与居一焉。或坐而论道，或作而行之，或审曲面执，以饬五材，以辨民器，或通四方之珍异以资之，或饬力以长地财，或治丝麻以成之。坐而论道，谓之王公；作而行之，谓之士大夫；审曲面执，以饬五材，以辨民器，谓之百工；通四方之珍异以资之，谓之商旅；饬力以长地财，谓之农夫；治丝麻以成之，谓之妇功。
粤无镈，燕无函，秦无庐，胡无弓车。粤之无镈也，非无镈也，夫人而能为镈也；燕之无函也，非无函也，夫人而能为函也；秦之无庐也，非无庐也，夫人而能为庐也；胡之无弓车也，非无弓车也，夫人而能为弓车也。
知者创物。巧者述之，守之世，谓之工。百工之事，皆圣人之作也。烁金以为刃，凝土以为器，作车以行陆，作舟以行水，此皆圣人之所作也。天有时，地有气，材有美，工有巧，合此四者，然后可以为良。材美工巧，然而不良，则不时，不得地气也。
橘逾淮而北为枳，𬸱鹆不逾济，貉逾汶则死，此地气然也。郑之刀，宋之斤，鲁之削，吴粤之剑，迁乎其地而弗能为良，地气然也。燕之角，荆之干，妢胡之笴，吴粤之金锡，此材之美者也。天有时以生，有时以杀；草木有时以生，有时以死；石有时以泐；水有时以凝，有时以泽，此天时也。凡攻木之工七，攻金之工六，攻皮之工五，设色之工五，刮摩之工五，抟埴之工二。攻木之工：轮、舆、弓、庐、匠、车、梓；攻金之工：筑、冶、凫、栗、叚、桃；攻皮之工：函、鲍、韗、韦、裘；设色之工：画、缋、钟、筐、㡛；刮摩之工：玉、栉、雕、矢、磬；抟埴之工：陶、瓬。有虞氏上陶，夏后氏上匠，殷人上梓，周人上舆。故一器而工聚焉者，车为多。车有六等之数：车轸四尺，谓之一等；戈柲六尺有六寸，既建而迆，崇于轸四尺，谓之二等；人长八尺，崇于戈四尺，谓之三等；殳长寻有四尺，崇于人四尺，谓之四等；车戟常，崇于殳四尺，谓之五等；酋矛常有四尺，崇于戟四尺，谓之六等。车谓之六等之数。凡察车之道，必自载于地者始也，是故察车自轮始。凡察车之道，欲其朴属而微至。不朴属，无以为完久也；不微至，无以为戚速也。轮已崇，则人不能登也；轮已庳，则于马终古登陀也。故兵车之轮六尺有六寸，田车之轮六尺有三寸，乘车之轮六尺有六寸。六尺有六寸之轮，轵崇三尺有三寸也，加轸与𫐗焉，四尺也。人长八尺，登下以为节。
轮人为轮，斩三材必以其时。三材既具，巧者和之。毂也者，以为利转也；辐也者，以为直指也；牙也者，以为固抱也。轮敝，三材不失职，谓之完。望而视其轮，欲其幎尔而下迆也。进而视之，欲其微至也。无所取之，取诸圜也。望其幅，欲其揱尔而纤也；进而视之，欲其肉称也，无所取之，取诸易直也。望其毂，欲其眼也，进而视之，欲其帱之廉也，无所取之，取诸急也。视其缏，欲其蚤之正也。察其菑蚤不齵，则轮虽敝不匡。凡斩毂之道，必矩其阴阳。阳也者稹理而坚，阴也者疏理而柔。是故以火养其阴，而齐诸其阳，则毂虽敝不藃。毂小而长则柞，大而短则挚。是故六分其轮崇，以其一为之牙围，参分其牙围，而漆其二。椁其漆内而中诎之，以为之毂长，以其长为之围，以其围之阞捎其薮。五分其毂之长，去一以为贤，去三以为轵。容毂必直，陈篆必正，施胶必厚，施筋必数，帱必负干。既摩，革色青白，谓之毂之善。参分其毂长，二在外，一在内，以置其辐。凡辐，量其凿深以为辐广。辐广而凿浅，则是以大扤，虽有良工，莫之能固。凿深而辐小，则是固有余而强不足也。故竑其辐广以为之弱，则虽有重任，毂不折。
……

zh:
千年文宗，自圣人始，几易其名，多改其址，传道授业，不改其志，文脉不绝，绵延后世。
欲知大道，必先知史。今录十相事，补文津馆所未载。文心热血，皆作纸上书。
……
天佑二年，白马之变。长安文津馆遭朱贼屠戮，十相俱没。前人之事，实不可追，谓为憾事。
……
长乐老，旧姓冯，瀛洲人士，其先耕读传家……长安一诺，寻觅九经于乱世，颠沛半生而无悔……九经既得，雕为印版，流布天下，后进赖之……故择青州之良土，建馆藏书，开阁授业……千秋文脉，得以留存，文宗盛名，得以再兴……事四朝，相六帝，时人谓之“不忠”，然其为相二十余年，以持重镇俗为己任，未尝以片简扰于诸侯，承先人遗志，集散佚群典，传诸经于世，开教化之源，岂世俗所知耶?
……
道济先生，旧姓魏，卫州人士，幼孤贫，辞母谒洛阳……入文津馆，得长乐老亲传，以文宗事相托，为二代文元……契丹入中原，随众北上……建春秋别馆，纳南下流民……出文津馆，聚天下英才十六，缔三十年之盟约……
……
……本姓柴，邢州人士，器貌英奇，善骑射，寡言持重……道济先生故交，荐入文津馆，为二代武元……
……
林险生，建阳人士，南唐世家子，少有辩才，时人皆谓之麒麟儿……时国土崩裂，南北文坛相争，南派文人以建阳林氏、萧氏为首……开运三年，与世交萧氏鹤衣结伴北上，赴中渡桥退外敌……入文津馆，师承十相……世宗南征，随军南下，游说诸世家故旧，“纸片渡江”，藏书合楼，为十相推举，成三代文元……开百日筵，辩天下人，诸名儒大家奉其为文坛之首，此后凡著书立说，皆以笔录抄送文津馆为荣……
……
（此篇中唯道济先生、柴武元事迹有大段篇幅被墨汁遮掩，尤其柴武元，其名号称谓皆从实录中隐去，不知何故。）
en:
A millennium of literary heritage, beginning with the Sages. It has changed its name several times and altered its location frequently; yet in transmitting the Dao and imparting knowledge, it has never changed its resolve. The lineage of letters remains unbroken, stretching endlessly into future generations. To understand the Great Way, one must first know history. Today, I record the deeds of the Ten Sages to supplement what is unrecorded in the annals of the Inkbound Order. The literary heart and the hot blood are all set down as words upon the paper.
...
In the second year of Tianyou, the Baima Incident occurred. The Inkbound Order in Chang'an was slaughtered by the rebel Zhu, and the Ten Sages all perished. The affairs of our predecessors are truly beyond recovery, deemed an eternal regret.
...
Elder Changle, whose former surname was Feng, a native of Yingzhou. His ancestors passed down the traditions of farming and studying... A single promise in Chang'an led him to seek the Nine Classics amidst a chaotic world, enduring half a lifetime of wandering without regret... Once the Nine Classics were obtained, they were carved into printing blocks and distributed throughout the realm, upon which later scholars relied... Therefore, he chose the fertile soil of Qingzhou to build the Order and house the books, opening pavilions to teach... The literary lineage of a thousand autumns was thus preserved, and the grand name of the literary sect was able to rise again... He served four dynasties and was a minister to six emperors. The people of his time called him "disloyal," yet during his twenty-odd years as a minister, he took it upon himself to maintain stability and soothe the populace. Never once did he disturb the regional lords with a single slip of a decree. He inherited the dying wishes of his predecessors, gathered scattered ancient tomes, transmitted the various classics to the world, and opened the source of enlightenment. How could the mundane world ever comprehend this?
...
Master Daoji's former surname was Wei, and he was a native of Weizhou. Orphaned and impoverished in his youth, he bid farewell to his mother and paid respects in Luoyang... He entered the Inkbound Order, received the direct teachings of Elder Changle, was entrusted with the affairs of the literary sect, and became the Second Laureate... When the Khitan invaded the Central Plains, he followed the masses north... He established the Spring and Autumn Annex, taking in refugees fleeing south... He departed the Inkbound Order, gathered sixteen supreme talents of the realm, and forged a thirty-year covenant...
...
[Text heavily obscured]... Original surname Chai, a native of Xingzhou. Striking and heroic in appearance, skilled in horseback archery, reticent yet steadfast... An old friend of Daoji, recommended to enter the Inkbound Order, becoming the Second Champion...
...
Lin Xiansheng, a native of Jianyang, a son of a noble house of the Southern Tang. He possessed great eloquence in his youth; the people of his time all called him the Young Luminary... At that time, the territory was fractured, and the northern and southern literary circles clashed. The southern scholars were led by the Lin and Xiao clans of Jianyang... In the third year of Kaiyun, he traveled north with his family friend, Xiao Heyi, journeying to Zhongdu Bridge to repel foreign enemies... He entered the Inkbound Order, apprenticing under the Ten Sages... When Emperor Shizong marched south, he followed the army, persuading old friends among the noble houses. "Crossing the river on slips of paper," he merged the libraries and pavilions. Recommended by the Ten Sages, he became the Third Laureate... He held a hundred-day banquet, debating the scholars of the realm. Various great Confucian masters revered him as the head of the literary world. Thereafter, whenever anyone wrote a book or established a theory, they considered it an honor to hand-copy their work and send it to the Inkbound Order...
(Note: In this chapter, only the deeds of Master Daoji and Champion Chai have large sections obscured by ink. Especially regarding Champion Chai, his titles and appellations have been erased from the veritable records, for reasons unknown.)

打听了一嘴，才知这历城台虽是文津馆的演武之所，却不曾封闭，常有乡人来此锻炼，引弓习射，以图拒匪。
我此番来，正赶上三年一度的傲林匹敌车赛，五湖四海的参赛者都聚集于此。一位文津馆的小夫子跟我说，这车赛起源于周礼，三人一乘，左弓右矛，中御马。听闻文津馆可以追至春秋，也不知是不是从那时一路传下来的？
……嗨呀！可气！方才拉了两个临时凑的乡亲去那车赛，头一轮便败下阵来。在家时姊姊总笑我四肢不勤，今日一试，果然不假！如今正得悻悻坐在横杠底下写这几笔，只求杠上那位老伯抓稳些，莫要砸在我天灵盖上……
好了，就此搁笔。打磨筋骨去也！
en:
What a vast expanse at the foot of Mount Tai! The people here possess an extraordinary vigor. Pacing the tracks, practicing fist forms, vaulting bars, and driving chariots, every one of them is dripping with sweat. Even the elders, women, and children in this territory seem to have sturdier bones and tougher sinews than those elsewhere. Had I not spotted a ragged, panting line of young pedagogues from the Inkbound Order trailing at the edge of the grounds, I would have suspected I had wandered into the wrong realm entirely, rather than the Martial Hall of the Inkbound Order!
After asking around, I learned that although Licheng Terrace is the martial arena of the Inkbound Order, it has never been closed off. Locals frequently come here to temper their bodies, drawing bows and practicing archery to fend off bandits.
As fortune would have it, my visit coincided with the triennial Crownleek Tournament, drawing competitors from the five lakes and four seas. A young scholar of the Order told me this chariot race traces its origins back to The Rites of Zhou: three men to a chariot, an archer on the left, a spearman on the right, and a driver in the center. Hearing that the Inkbound Order's lineage could be traced back to the Spring and Autumn Period, I could not help but wonder if this tradition truly survived intact all the way from that ancient era.
Sigh! How infuriating! Just moments ago, I dragged two hastily assembled villagers to join the chariot race, only to suffer a crushing defeat in the very first round. When at home, my elder sister always mocked me for being a stranger to physical toil. Testing my mettle today, I see her words ring entirely true! And so, I am left to sit resentfully beneath this horizontal bar, writing down these few lines, praying only that the old gentleman swinging above grips the wood tightly, lest he crash down upon the crown of my head.
Enough. I lay down my brush here. Off I go to temper my bones and sinews!
Which bastard hit me from behind?!

en:
That man once said to Tian Ying that there is a task so grave, it will condemn them beyond redemption. 

At the time, many used religion as a shield, hiding behind faith to escape taxes, wearing monks' robes while committing wicked deeds. To suppress these false monks and destroy their idols was to serve the greater good. 
To purge the evil and unmask the lies, that was the great task. To shatter a thousand golden Buddhas, that was the path to damnation. 
Can you do something so blasphemous, for the sake of righteousness? 
I will go. 
Tian Guang once slit his throat to spur Jing Ke on his mission. What would you give up for the cause? 
I too would slit my throat 
And so, Tian Ying vanished from the world. In his place, the monk Miaoshan was born. 

Though he had never truly believed in the Buddha. 
To feed himself to tigers, if that is what it takes, so be it. 
The man who sent him laughed, for Tian Ying already carry the heart of a Buddha.

可猫是猫，人是人，猫和人不应该有瓜葛。
而且，它只想做世界上跑得最快的，最自由的一只小猫。
可那胖厨子有一双世间最巧的手，能做出世间最美味的鱼羹。
他还有一双世间最干净的眼睛。那双眼睛注视它，却从不试图驯养它。
所以乘风留下了。
只是暂时留下。乘风心想。
en:
The name Windrider was given to her by the fat cook in the house. She doesn't like it.

But cats are cats, and humans are humans. There should be no entanglements. 
All she wants is to be the fastest, freest cat in the world. 
But the fat cook has the most skillful hands in the world, he makes the most delicious fish stew. 
He also has the cleanest eyes in the world. Eyes that see her, but never try to tame her. 
So Windrider stayed. 
Just for now, she thought.

从有记忆起，阿黑就和阿白待在一块。阿白遇到什么好吃的，会给阿黑分一口；阿白在哪，阿黑就要跟到哪。
所以当阿白决定逃出栾城的时候，阿黑想都没想，就跟着跑了出来。逃到一半，他们迎面撞上了从前在城里见过的人，阿黑没搞明白，这些人逃了出来，为何又想回头？看见那些人往阿白身上挂的信，阿黑算是明白了三分。
既是阿白决定帮助送信，阿黑也不能闲着。它一身黑，跑得又快，外加阿白能为它做掩护，当然有用武之地。
自此，每逢夜晚，栾城之外就多了两个一黑一白的矫健身影。
en:
For as long as he could remember, Shadow had been with Snowy. If Snowy found something tasty, she'd share a bite with Shadow; wherever Snowy went, Shadow followed.
So when Snowy decided to flee Luancheng, Shadow followed without a second thought. Halfway through, they ran into people they had seen in the city before. Why did these people want to go back after escaping? Shadow didn't understand. But when he saw the letters they tied to Snowy, he understood a little.
Since Snowy decided to help deliver letters, Shadow couldn't stay idle. He was pitch black and fast, and with Snowy providing a distraction, he certainly had a role to play.
From then on, every night, two agile figures, one black and one white, appeared outside Luancheng.

zh:
然而时局总是崩坏得很快，明宗的病逝拉开了皇权纷争的序幕。眼看着石敬瑭割下燕云十六州换来契丹增援，挥师洛阳，京城一片大乱，众人纷纷外逃，此时偏往皇城逆行的王大演自然十分惹眼。
“叶不休——叶不休——”王大演声嘶力竭地呼唤。他遥遥看到玄武楼起火，不由愈发担心朋友的安危。
“咳咳……我在这里……”虚弱而熟悉的声音从护城河方向飘来，不是叶不休又是谁？
王大演好不容易将人捞上来，对方不先感激，倒是急着翻看怀中藏着的纸包，见里面裹着的棋谱安然无恙，方才松了口气。
“你怎么掉河里的？”王大演问。
“别提了，倒霉。出城门时着急，被人搡着，一下子栽进去了。好在我用油纸包住了棋谱，又会凫水，才等到你来，保住了我的心血。总之，这次谢了！“
叶不休难得语气诚恳，惹得王大演很不习惯，他忍不住揉揉耳朵，别扭道：“哦，反正我也不是为了救你，只是为了那些记载着明宗征战的棋谱。”
看着王大演嘴硬的样子，叶不休忍不住畅快大笑出来，笑得人快恼了才停下，神色无比认真地说：“王大演，我们暂时别下棋了，为这些棋谱找一个英主，结束这个乱世吧！”
鬼使神差地，王大演答应了。他们没有武功，家当也不多，就凭着一股年轻的气性四处打探消息，奔着他们的目标头破血流地前行。他们不喜石敬瑭，便南下，可是却处处碰壁，屡屡失望。后来听说晋朝出了一个叫王清的英雄，两人又折身北上，只恨走得太慢，还未到达晋朝边境就传来了王清身殒的消息。于是又是数年辗转蹉跎，已然年过不惑，他们终于再次找到一位英主——大周皇帝郭荣。他的北伐军如今驻扎在清河，而他们就在清河！然而这时的王大演却因为积年疲敝病倒了，等他再次醒来，便发现换了个地方。
en:
But situations changed fast. Emperor Mingzong passed away, and the court was soon thrown into turmoil. Shi Jingtang ceded the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun to the Khitan in exchange for military support, then turned his army toward Luoyang. The capital fell into chaos, and civilians fled in droves. Amid the uproar, Wang Dayan did the unthinkable, returning to the capital."Ye Buxiu! Ye Buxiu!" he called, his voice hoarse with desperation. In the distance, the Black Tortoise Tower was burning, and his worry deepened.
"*Coughs*... I'm here..." came a faint, familiar voice from somewhere near the moat. Who else could it be but Ye Buxiu?
Soaked and shivering, Ye Buxiu was hauled from the water. But instead of expressing gratitude, the first thing he did was check the paper parcel clutched to his chest. Only when he was sure the chess manual inside, was intact did he finally breathe a sigh of relief.
"How in the world did you end up in the moat?" Wang Dayan asked.
"Don't bring it up! I was rushing out through the city gate, got shoved in the chaos, and splashed. Bad luck, really. Good thing I wrapped the manual in oil paper. And I can swim. So, yeah. Managed to hold on until you showed up. Anyway, thanks!" 
The sincerity in his voice threw Wang Dayan off balance. He scratched his ear, awkward as ever, "I didn't come to save you. It was for the chess manual. You know that."
Seeing Wang Dayan being so stubborn, Ye Buxiu couldn't help but laugh heartily, stopping only when it was getting too much. Then he said with a serious look, "Dayan, this isn't the time to be playing chess. We need to find a ruler worthy of these manuals and bring this chaos to an end."
To his own surprise, Wang Dayan agreed. They had no martial skills, no great wealth, but they had youth and ambition. So the two set off in search of a worthy ruler, pressing forward through hardships and hunger. They didn't like Shi Jingtang, so they headed south, only to meet one dead end after another. Eventually, news reached them of a rising hero in the Jin Dynasty named Wang Qing. Full of hope, they turned north again. But they were too late. By the time they reached the Jin border, word came: Wang Qing was dead. And so, after years of drifting and missed opportunities, they had already passed the age of Enlightenment. At last, they found a new hero: Emperor Guo Rong (Emperor Shizong) of the Later Zhou Dynasty. His northern expedition army had already marched to Qinghe, right where they were. But years of hardship had worn Wang Dayan down. He fell ill. And when he finally opened his eyes, he found himself in a place he didn't recognize.

You six leaders of my forces, I hereby swear and declare to you: The Youhu clan has insolently insulted the Five Elements, and has willfully abandoned the three cardinal virtues. zh:
“师傅，你跟寒娘子，究竟是什么关系啊？”
天不收不急不忙地把手中的药典放下。
“这么好奇？那师父的绝学你好不好奇？”
窦豆豆头一缩，手中的药杵像在捣蒜：“不好奇不好奇。师傅——好了，我不问了。再不成亲师父老了就得跟我住了……”
“变成一个孤寡老人，太可怜了。”
豆豆在非常大声地“小声”嘟囔，连带姚药药也低头作了下鬼脸。
天不收懒得逗徒弟了。洛神是不会老的，洛神的船夫也是。
就算七老八十了， 他俩照样是黄河上一对神仙搭档。
不过这两个半大小孩，年纪不大，好奇心倒是不小。成天四处打听……和不羡仙里的那个有的一比。
要不是当年见寒香寻养了孩子，自己也不会一时心软也捡了这俩。儿女徒弟都是债。
想到此处，天不收又支起身子，端起作师父的风范。
“药典背完了吗？账簿理完了吗？我考考你俩，昨日风痹的病人，应以茯苓、防风，白术几两入药？”
天不收素来没什么严师风范，此刻两徒弟也只是讨好地嘿嘿一笑，再不说话。只是手上的动作又快了几分。

不羡仙有传言，活人医馆的天不收大夫对不羡仙酒馆的老板娘，肯定有那么些不一般。
看诊的病人明里暗里向天不收大夫求证，天不收只是笑笑，偶尔露出为之神伤的表情。
良好的人缘，足以让天不收在这十几年里和江无浪竞争不羡仙上门婿的位置。
以这种方式扯上关联，总也好过天河分楚汉，清清白白，似两条永不相靠的线。

“今日之事，不同之前的生意，你我切记不能有一丝泄露出去。”
给燕北盟做了那单大生意之后，她低声交代，凑得很近。
温润的火光拂过她的脸颊，这井下阴风处原来也不冷。
他应答，勾起嘴角，笑得和煦。
这单摆渡钱早就送在井下，他一点也不关心。反而她和褚清泉闹掰的戏份，天不收毫不掩饰地站在那里看了全场。
愚蠢，可他心底有隐秘的快乐。
他们之间的秘密越多，仿佛就越亲密无间。
她只信任他。
他知道不为人知的她的一面，比任何人多。比褚清泉多。

只是，那一天的她，他从未见过。
他见她把一坛又一坛酒倒入湖中，不停息的酒液，不知怎的，他觉得像她的眼泪。
她沉默地望着泛起涟漪的水面。
天不收一直在远处。
这辈子，只有洛神的“船夫”不会离开她，风雨共渡。
只要她肯回头看看。

只是她从不曾回头。
不管是不羡仙精明爽利的老板，弱水岸执刀换脸的洛神。
还是此刻的河边……一个缅怀过去，为情伤心的女人。
就像这十几年每夜睡在井下，仔细伪装成男人的天不收自己一样。


他们可以是传言中关系匪浅的天大夫和寒老板，也可以是不为人知的江湖共犯。
还可以是邻里乡亲口中想要凑成一对的“郎”才女貌。
但他们永远不可能在一起。
这世上，两个女人的心，只能无限接近，然后停在一尺的亲密距离。
最遥远的距离。
en:
"Master, what's going on between you and Madam Han?"
Unfated Tian set down the medical book, unhurried as ever.
"That's what you care about? Not my secret skills?"
Dou Doudou shrank back, grinding his pestle like he was smashing garlic. "Nope, not interested, not at all. Master—okay, I'll stop asking. If you never get married, you'll be stuck living with me when you're old..."
"Just an old bachelor, how tragic."
Doudou muttered loudly, and Yaoyao made a face.

Unfated Tian didn't bother teasing them further. The Water Lady and her boatman would never grow old; even at eighty, they'd still be the legendary pair on the river.
But these two kids—young, curious, always poking their noses into things—reminded him of another troublemaker back at Blissful Retreat.
If he hadn't seen Han Xiangxun raising a child years ago, he probably wouldn't have softened and taken these two in.
Kids and apprentices always come with strings attached.
Thinking of this, he straightened his back and put on his "master" face.
"Have you memorized the medical book? Balanced the accounts? Let's see: for yesterday's patient with joint pain, how much poria, saposhnikovia, and atractylodes do you add to the prescription?"
Unfated Tian was never one for strict discipline, so the two apprentices just grinned sheepishly and set to work faster.

Rumor had it around Blissful Retreat that Doctor Tian from Evercare Clinic and the owner of the tavern had something special between them.
Sometimes, patients would ask him about it—some outright, some just hinting. Unfated Tian would only smile, sometimes with a hint of sadness.
His friendly ways had put him in playful competition with Jiang Wulang for the role of Han Xiangxun's husband—all because whoever married her would get to help run the tavern.
People always found ways to connect them, and it was far better than living as strangers, never crossing paths.

"Today's job isn't like the usual. Not a word about this to anyone."
After they'd done that big job for Northern Vow, Han Xiangxun had leaned in close, her voice low and serious. The firelight warmed her face, making the cold underground seem less harsh.

Unfated Tian only smiled, gentle as ever. The money for ferrying souls had long since gone—it didn't matter to him.
What did matter was watching Han Xiangxun split with Chu Qingquan. Unfated Tian hadn't bothered hiding that he watched the whole thing.
Maybe it was foolish, but he felt a secret happiness.
The more secrets they shared, the closer they felt.
She trusted him, and he knew more about her hidden side than anyone else—more even than Chu Qingquan.

But that day, she was someone he'd never seen before.
He watched her pour jar after jar of wine into the lake; the endless stream looked like tears she refused to shed.
She stared at the ripples in silence.
Unfated Tian kept his distance.
In this life, only the Water Lady's boatman would never leave her—through all the storms, always there, if only she would turn and look.
But she never did.
Not as the sharp, capable owner of Blissful Retreat, not as the Water Lady with a new face, knife in hand by the river.
Not even now, by the water's edge—a woman mourning the past, heartbroken for love.
Just like Unfated Tian, who spent every night in the well, carefully disguising as a man.
They could be the doctor and tavern owner people whispered about, secret partners in the underworld, or the "perfect couple" the neighbors tried to match up.
But they could never truly be together.
In the end, two hearts could come as close as possible, but always stop just short—close enough to almost touch, forever a step apart.
Those stuffy scholars are making a terrible racket!

zh:

此言禹之事，吾今行兼矣。
en:
In ancient times, Yu the Great governed the realm by taming the waters. To the west, he carved out the Western River and Yudou to drain the Great Waters; to the north, he raised dams at Fangyuan and Gushui to divert the floods, splitting the streams at Mount Dizhu and cutting through the Dragon Gate to benefit the peoples of Yan, Dai, Hu, Mo, and the Western River. In the east, he drained the stagnant lands, contained the Mengzhu Marshes, and channeled the waters into nine streams to secure the eastern territories, bringing prosperity to the people of Jizhou. To the south, he guided the Yangtze, Han, Huai, and Ru rivers eastward into the Five Lakes, bestowing his grace upon the peoples of Jing, Chu, Yu, Yue, and the southern tribes.

Such were the deeds of Yu. Today, I seek to follow his example, to practice the Way of Universal Love.

It was an ancient spiritual practice for warding off bad luck.

zh:
被撩湖兵捡起的时候，旺旺还是一只比巴掌大不了多少的小狗崽。
那天早上，湖边的风潮湿得很，兵士们正撑着竿划开水面。
每天，他们都要将沉重的葑草连同淤泥一点点从湖底拔起，再运到岸上。

忽然，浅滩的草妖风似的抖了几抖。
不是抓鱼的水獭，也不是带着雏鸭早起的野鸭。
一只满脸泥土的小狗探出头来，只有眼睛还亮亮的。

老兵阿洪放下手里的长竹竿，蹚着没过小腿的凉水走了过去。
小家伙冻得没力气了，任由一双布满老茧的大手把它捞了起来。

回到营地，兵士们凑了一碗温热的鱼汤，泡上软烂的碎米。
小家伙闻到香味，连滚带爬地扑进碗里，吃得吧唧作响，连鼻尖上都沾着米粒。
吃饱喝足后，它嗅嗅大伙的靴子，中气十足地叫了两声。
“这小东西，嗓门倒挺旺。咱们这撩湖的苦差事，就缺个兴旺的兆头，以后就叫你旺旺吧！”

西湖春有烟柳夏有荷，秋枫冬雪，更是美不胜收。
旺旺喜欢湖上的景象，但它和阿洪等千名撩湖兵一样，更在意今日清理了多少葑草淤泥。
当兵士们一解开船绳，它就摇着尾巴跟上，稳稳地坐在船头。
旺旺紧紧盯着水面，俨然一位尽职尽责的小监工。
今日湖上的风携着丝丝小雨，落在水面泛起涟漪，也把旺旺的耳朵吹得向后翻起。
此风此雨，仿佛能绵延千万年。
en:
When the Dredging Corps first picked him up, Bountiful was a pup barely bigger than a hand.
The wind off the lake was damp that morning, and the soldiers were pushing their poles through the water.
Every day, they hauled heavy weed and silt up from the lakebed, bit by bit, and carried it ashore.

Suddenly, the reeds along the shallows shivered, like some strange wind had gone through them.
Not an otter after fish, nor a wild duck out early with her ducklings.
A puppy poked his head out, face caked in mud, only his eyes still shining bright.

Hong, a veteran, set down his long bamboo pole and waded through the cold water up past his shins.
The pup was too frozen to move, and a pair of big, calloused hands scooped him up.

Back at the camp, the soldiers put together a bowl of warm fish broth with soft broken rice in it.
Catching the scent, the pup tumbled straight into the bowl, slurping and smacking away, grains of rice stuck to the tip of his nose.
Once he'd eaten his fill, he sniffed everyone's boots and let out two hearty barks.
"Listen to those lungs. Dredging is miserable work, and we could use a sign of good fortune. We'll call you Bountiful, then."

West Lake has its misty willows in spring, lotus in summer, maples in autumn, snow in winter. Each season more beautiful than the last.
Bountiful loves the sights of the lake, but like Hong and the thousand other Dredging Corps soldiers, he cares more about how much weed and silt got cleared that day.
The moment the soldiers untie the boat, he wags his tail and follows along, settling himself firmly at the bow.
Bountiful keeps his eyes fixed on the water, every bit the dutiful little supervisor.
The wind over the lake carries a drizzle today, dimpling the water and folding Bountiful's ears back.
This wind, this rain... it feels as though they could go on for ten thousand years.

Preparing the master copy was the first major step in woodblock printing. A skilled scribe transcribed the text onto fine paper in neat regular script, producing the model from which the block would be carved. 【下经·䷟】

䷟
恒：亨，无咎，利贞，利有攸往。
彖曰：恒，久也。刚上而柔下，雷风相与，巽而动，刚柔皆应，恒。恒亨无咎利贞”，久于其道也。天地之道，恒久而不已也。利有攸往”，终则有始也。日月得天而能久照，四时变化而能久成。圣人久于其道而天下化成。观其所恒，而天地万物之情可见矣。
《象》曰：雷风，恒。君子以立不易方。
初六：浚恒，贞凶，无攸利。
《象》曰：“浚恒”之“凶”，始求深也。
九二：悔亡。
《象》曰：九二“悔亡”，能久中也。
九三：不恒其德，或承之羞，贞吝。
《象》曰：“不恒其德”，无所容也。
九四：田无禽。
《象》曰：久非其位，安得禽也！
六五：恒其德，贞，妇人吉，夫子凶。
《象》曰：妇人贞吉，从一而终也。夫子制义，从妇凶也。
上六：振恒，凶。
《象》曰：振恒在上，大无功也。
en:
【Lower Canon·䷟】

䷟
Heng (Duration): Prosperity and success. No blame. It is favorable to be steadfast and upright. It is favorable to have somewhere to go.
The Commentary on the Decision says: Heng means duration. The strong is above and the weak is below; thunder and wind act in mutual accord; the yielding follows the moving; the strong and the weak all respond to each other—this is Heng. "Heng: prosperity and success, no blame, favorable to be steadfast and upright"—this means enduring in one's Dao. The way of Heaven and Earth is to endure forever without ceasing. "Favorable to have somewhere to go"—at the end there is a beginning. The Sun and Moon, receiving Heaven's light, can shine forever; the four seasons, through their changes, can bring things to completion forever. The Emperor, enduring in his Dao, transforms all under Heaven. Observing what endures, the true nature of Heaven, Earth, and all things can be seen.
The Image says: Thunder and wind—this is Heng. The noble person, standing firm, does not change his direction.
First Six: Deeply seeking duration—steadfastness brings misfortune. Nothing is favorable.
The Image says: The "misfortune" of "deeply seeking duration" comes from seeking too deeply at the start.
Nine in the Second: Regret disappears.
The Image says: Nine in the Second's "regret disappears" because it can endure in the central position.
Nine in the Third: Not enduring one's virtue may bring shame upon oneself. Steadfastness brings humiliation.
The Image says: "Not enduring one's virtue" leaves no place to be accepted.
Nine in the Fourth: In the field, there is no game.
The Image says: Long in a position not its own—how can it obtain game?
Six in the Fifth: Enduring one's virtue—steadfastness. For a Woman, good fortune; for a man, misfortune.
The Image says: The Woman's steadfastness brings good fortune, for she follows one to the Final Day. The man must govern by Righteousness; following a Woman brings misfortune.
Top Six: Shaking duration—misfortune.
The Image says: Shaking duration while at the top brings no great achievement.

zh: 成于唐代，李翰所撰。书名取诸《周易·蒙卦》“匪我求童蒙，童蒙求我”之义。全书四言成句，两句一韵，上下对偶，各述一典。所录自春秋至南北朝，约六百人，事迹涉政治、军事、文化、方术，包罗甚广。敦煌莫高窟出土唐代抄本残卷，为今存最早版本。
en: Authored by Li Han during the Tang dynasty. The title is drawn from the Book of Changes, specifically the Hexagram of Youthful Folly, which states: "It is not I who seek the young fool; it is the young fool who seeks me." The entire book is written in four-character lines, with rhymes every two lines and elegant antithetical couplets. Each line recounts a specific historical allusion. It chronicles roughly six hundred figures from the Spring and Autumn period down to the Northern and Southern Dynasties. The events covered span politics, warfare, culture, and esoteric arts, making it astonishingly comprehensive. A fragmentary Tang dynasty manuscript unearthed from the Mogao Caves in Dunhuang stands as its earliest surviving edition.

zh:
大家都说懒瓜是懒猫猫，平日除了吃就知道睡，就算被人从地上强行抱起来也能接着打呼噜。但饲猫人也知道，懒瓜是一只特别勇敢的小猫。
懒瓜生来就比别的小猫少了一趾，尾巴尖尖也是折断的，明显有些先天不足。但它自睁眼起就颇为好吃能吃，很快便将自己养成了滚圆的模样，叫大家渐渐遗忘了这点。
那日夜黑风高，陌生的气息闯入了饲猫人的屋舍。贪凉睡在院外的懒瓜睁开了金灿灿的双眼，在黑暗中静静地等待危险的逼近，而后——“喵嗷！”
静谧的夜里，小猫嘶吼声尤为骇人，将全院小猫与饲猫人都惊醒了。
待饲猫人冲到院内，看到地上凌乱的陌生足迹时才意识到有外人闯入，心急如焚地清点小猫时却发现懒瓜不见了。
焦心不已的饲猫人，四处寻觅，直至太阳升起仍未能寻到懒瓜的踪迹。就在饲猫人因担心其他小猫会遭遇类似危险不得不返回屋舍时，才发现懒瓜不知何时已出现在她的身后，一进院子便躺倒在地打呼噜，露出了带着几道伤痕的肚皮。
饲猫人抹了把脸，才一把将沉重得令人感到踏实心安的懒瓜抱起：“懒瓜懒瓜，你要吓死我了！”
懒瓜用爪子顶开越靠越近的饲猫人的大脸，大大地打了个哈欠。
en:
Everyone says Lazybones is a lazy cat through and through, doing nothing all day but eat and sleep. Even if you scoop it up off the ground by force, it'll keep right on purring in its sleep. But the cat-keeper knows better: Lazybones is, in truth, an especially brave little cat.
Lazybones was born with one toe fewer than the other kittens, and the tip of its tail was broken from birth too, clear signs that it came into the world a little lacking. But from the moment it first opened its eyes, it proved quite the eager eater, and soon enough had rounded itself out into such a plump little shape that everyone gradually forgot about it.
Then came a night of pitch darkness and howling wind, when an unfamiliar scent crept into the cat-keeper's home. Lazybones, who loved to sleep out in the cool air of the courtyard, opened its golden eyes and waited silently in the dark as the danger drew near. And then: "Meowrrr!"
In the hush of the night, the kitten's snarling cry was especially bloodcurdling, startling awake every cat in the courtyard along with the cat-keeper.
When the cat-keeper rushed out into the yard and saw the scattered, unfamiliar footprints upon the ground, she realized at once that an intruder had broken in. Her heart pounding, she counted the kittens in a panic, only to find that Lazybones was nowhere to be seen.
Frantic with worry, the cat-keeper searched high and low, but even as the sun rose, she found no trace of Lazybones. Just as she was forced to return to the house, fearing the other kittens might face similar danger, she turned to find Lazybones had somehow appeared right behind her all along. The moment she entered the yard, Lazybones flopped down onto the ground, purring away, revealing a belly marked with a few fresh wounds.
Wiping her face, the cat-keeper finally scooped up Lazybones, whose comforting weight settled her racing heart: "Lazybones, Lazybones, you nearly scared me to death!"
Lazybones pushed away the cat-keeper's face as it drew ever closer with one paw, and let out an enormous yawn.

#Y记：芳茝即白芷，今香料也。宿莽者，冬生不死之草也，其味辛香，可驱虫蠹。三闾大夫揽芳茝、搴宿莽，非采香草，乃修德洁志，为国效力、匡正气也。

en:
Spring breaks and the year opens, the white day stretches on and on.
I shall let my spirit wander and find joy, following the Jiang Xia to ease my sorrows.
I gather the fragrant angelica of the great marshes, and pluck the Wintergrass from the long isle.

—Qu Yuan, "Longing for the Fair One"

#YAnnotation: Fragrant angelica is a white herb, prized today as a spice. The Wintergrass is a plant that grows through winter and does not die. Pungent and aromatic, it drives away insects and rot. When Master Qu gathered fragrant angelica and plucked the Wintergrass, it is not truly the gathering of herbs. It is the cultivation of virtue, the purification of will, the serving of one's realm, and the upholding of righteousness.
The hardships of man are limited. Let us await the days to come... for even one as deeply grieved as Master Qu may yet pluck fragrance and ease his sorrow.#E

Under your orders, we slipped into that sealed-off valley under the cover of night the day before yesterday. With patrols pacing the entrance, ordinary methods wouldn't have gotten us very far. Fortunately, before we set out, we dug up a Qiongqi Artificer mask we had seized previously. The journey was thrilling but safe, and we managed to sneak deep into the valley.
Piled up there are objects that shouldn't exist in such a place, and faintly, we could see several iron doors that have never been opened. There is no telling what is hidden inside. 【三年问第三十八】

三年之丧何也？曰：称情而立文，因以饰群，别亲疏贵践之节，而不可损益也。故曰：无易之道也。创巨者其日久，痛甚者其愈迟，三年者，称情而立文，所以为至痛极也。斩衰苴杖，居倚庐，食粥，寝苫枕块，所以为至痛饰也。三年之丧，二十五月而毕；哀痛未尽，思慕未忘，然而服以是断之者，岂不送死者有已，复生有节哉？凡生天地之间者，有血气之属必有知，有知之属莫不知爱其类；今是大鸟兽，则失丧其群匹，越月逾时焉，则必反巡，过其故乡，翔回焉，鸣号焉，蹢躅焉，踟蹰焉，然后乃能去之；小者至于燕雀，犹有啁噍之顷焉，然后乃能去之；故有血气之属者，莫知于人，故人于其亲也，至死不穷。将由夫患邪淫之人与，则彼朝死而夕忘之，然而从之，则是曾鸟兽之不若也，夫焉能相与群居而不乱乎？将由夫修饰之君子与，则三年之丧，二十五月而毕，若驷之过隙，然而遂之，则是无穷也。故先王焉为之立中制节，壹使足以成文理，则释之矣。
……

音音是只耳朵很灵的猫，能分辨出不同娘子与宫人的脚步声。每回听清了人故作聪明的蹑手蹑脚，音音便会停下舔毛，预备着绕到来客脚边蹭蹭。
有娘子宠爱它，练琴也带着它，谁知接连弹错三次后，音音一跃而起，跳上了琴面。它收起爪尖，只留肉垫，轻轻一勾琴弦，余音袅袅，在琴声将尽之刻，音音长喵一声，再弹一声，弹琴复长喵，一战成名。
从此，来来往往的娘子与宫人，无人不晓音音大名——这是一只会弹琴的小猫，若你琴艺不行，也可以拜它为师，送些零嘴做束脩便好。
在猫数不清的日子里，也不知什么时候，娘子不再带着音音弹琴了，笑容也少了许多，音音常瞧见她对着花树发怔，念叨着诸如“前朝”“旧人”的话……不再靠近琴，它好像又变回了一只普通的，只是耳朵灵些的猫。
en:
Yinyin is a cat with remarkably sharp ears. It can tell different ladies and palace servants apart just by the sound of their footsteps.

Whenever it catches someone trying to be clever and tiptoe around, it pauses mid-groom, ready to circle over and rub against the visitor's ankles.

One lady doted on it so much that she even brought it along to practice the guqin. Then came the day she hit three wrong notes in a row. Yinyin sprang onto the instrument, tucked its claws away, and hooked a string with nothing but its paw pads.

The sound lingered. Right as the last note was about to fade, Yinyin let out a long meow and plucked one more note.
Meow, pluck. Pluck, meow.
Just like that, it became famous.

After that, every lady and servant who came and went knew the name Yinyin: a kitten that could "play" the guqin. If your playing was not up to scratch, you could even ask it to be your teacher. A few snacks as a token fee would do.

Days passed, too many to count. At some point, the lady stopped bringing Yinyin to the guqin. She smiled less. Yinyin often saw her staring at the flowering trees, murmuring things like "the former court" and "old faces"...

Yinyin no longer went near the instrument.
It seemed to turn back into an ordinary cat again, just one with especially keen ears.

zh:
陈途这一生，迈过很多坎。
从前为了进墨门，他熬过无数个油灯燃尽的夜晚。入门后，为了研究，他又日日夜夜地埋首机关之内。后来，他决定回乡，曾经迈过的坎，又成了一道新的难关。
可到底还是迈过来了，从前的坎儿都像是云烟散去，只留下那件代表墨门的弟子服，算是一个证见。

陈途本想着，就这样把那衣裳带走，带到坟堆里——
可一转念，想到他的弟子，那个寡言少语的傻小子。
除了这件衣裳，自己也没什么可以给他留下的物件。
陈途又把衣服包起来，放到了一边。
那小子，还没去过墨城呐。
毕竟这衣裳也算墨城的旧物，权当是个念想。
不过，往后要是那小子不想去也不打紧。
每个人都有自己的坎儿要过，而他，只是那小子人生某一段路途里的引路人。

小子！往前走诶！
或许有一天，那傻小子迈过了不同的坎儿，看到了更美的风景。
只期望到那时……这件破旧的弟子服，能代他陪在傻小子身边。
en:
Chen Tu had spent his entire life crossing one hurdle after another.

In the past, to join the Mohists, he had endured countless nights studying until his oil lamp burned dry. After entering the sect, he buried himself in the study of mechanics day and night. Later, when he decided to return home, the hurdles he had already crossed became entirely new challenges.
But he had crossed them all in the end. All those past hardships had faded away like smoke, leaving behind only his worn Mohist disciple's robe as a quiet testament to his journey.

At first, Chen Tu had planned to simply take the robe with him to the grave.
But on second thought, he remembered his apprentice, that quiet, silly lad.
Aside from this robe, he really had nothing else of value to leave behind for the boy.
So, Chen Tu folded the robe carefully and set it aside.

That kid hadn't even been to Mohist City yet. Since this robe was a relic of the city, it could serve as a keepsake.
And if the boy decided he didn't want to go in the future, that was fine too.
Everyone has their own hurdles to cross in life. Chen Tu was merely a guide for one short stretch of the boy's journey.

Keep moving forward, kid!
Perhaps one day, that silly lad would cross his own hurdles and see even more beautiful sights.
Chen Tu only hoped that when that time came, this tattered disciple's robe could keep the boy company in his stead.

zh:
“哟，向契丹投降，那不是跪着狗叫吗？要我、别说我，要是我爹干了这档子事，我可还能抬起头来，不像是别的狗崽子——”石贞站得很远，但也无用，他们念着这些话走过来，从他的肩膀撞过去，将他手上的药瓶撞到在地：“哟，何、哦不、石贞啊。”
他的拳头，捏紧了，再又松开。
就算他的拳头在这一刻落在他们的身上，就算将他们打倒在地，又有什么用呢。

他爹何徽临阵投降，跪倒在地的那个瞬间，最终压在了他身上，压了许多年，压到他从何贞变成了石贞。
他们说的是实话，拳头是打不碎实话的。

他一言不发，听他们的脚步走远，砸落在地的药瓶已经碎了，伤口重新崩裂出血迹。
不够疼。
军中多比武，也多有伤痛，但对于石贞而言，最疼的是往他肩头撞的那力道，那力道不轻不重，正好将他的身子撞偏几寸。
要契丹人的伤口，才盖得住这疼痛，要燕云十六州的土地，才能赢下重新将身子摆正的几寸力道。
会有那一天的。
他一生得要站两次，替父亲将跪下的那次站起来，再替自己站起来。
总会有那一天的。
名姓屈辱可洗，义父亦可以他为傲，他心中之人亦会与他并肩。
会有那一天的……一定会有那一天的。
en:
"Hey, surrendering to the Khitans, isn't that just crawling on all fours like a dog? Not just me, but if my dad did that, I'd never show my face again! Unlike some little pups..." Shi Zhen stood several paces away, but it didn't matter. The men sneered as they shouldered past him, knocking the medicine bottle from his hand. "Oops, He... no, it's Shi Zhen."
His fists clenched, then relaxed.
Even if he punched them right then, even if he beat them to the ground, what good would it do?

The moment his father, He Hui, had knelt in surrender on the battlefield had crushed him for years, grinding his name from He Zhen to Shi Zhen.
They spoke the truth, and fists couldn't shatter truth.

Silent, he listened as their footsteps faded. The fallen medicine bottle had shattered, reopening the wound on his arm.
It didn't hurt enough.
The army was full of brawls and injuries, but for Shi Zhen, the sharpest pain came from the shove that jostled his shoulder, just hard enough to knock him off balance.
Only Khitan blood could numb this ache. Only reclaiming the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun could give him the strength to stand upright again.
That day would come.
He would stand twice in his life: once to undo his father's kneel, once to stand for himself.
It will come.
A name's shame can be washed clean. His foster father will look at him with pride. The one who holds his heart will stand beside him.
That day would come... it had to.

侍御史沈公台鉴： 
 时维春令，岁在吉辰，萧某特遣愚帖，敬致问候于侍御史沈公尊前。
 久钦沈公之德望，今吾儿萧史得此机缘，能与令爱沈玉缔结秦晋之好，实乃萧府之幸，亦乃天作之合。
 犬子萧史，自幼秉承家训，文武兼备，品性高洁。然其现于军营之中，迟迟未得归家。
 其在军营，勤勉尽责，深得将士之敬爱。然婚姻大事，人生至要，萧某遣人告之，令其速速还家，以成佳偶。
 吾儿萧史对令爱沈玉倾慕已久，其之情深意切，天地可鉴。此番归家，定当与令爱共谐连理，琴瑟和鸣。
 萧某特以此帖，略表寸心，并致问候于沈公及府上诸位。愿两府情谊长存，共续华章。
 
 谨启。
 
 都指挥使 萧峻 敬上
en:
Honorable Censor Shen,
As spring blooms, I humbly send my warmest greetings.
Your virtue and reputation have long inspired our family. It's my honor to see my son's match with your beloved daughter—a union truly favored by heaven.
From youth, my son has honored our family's teachings, excelling in both scholarship and military service. I have urged him to come home to celebrate this union as soon as possible.
He's long admired your daughter, and together they will surely build a harmonious and joyful life.
With this letter, I convey my heartfelt intentions and warm regards to you and your family. May our families' bond grow ever stronger, and may our future be bright and prosperous.

Respectfully, 
Commander Xiao Jun

我有天志，可倚之服人。
世人多以为墨者行侠善使剑，却不知其更喜拳法。昔日，墨子弃儒立墨，常遭世人讥讽。墨子无惧，凡可理喻者则晓之以理，不可理喻者则饱以老拳。不曾想，世间愚人甚多，竟让墨子从中悟出一套拳法。
初创之时，此拳法甚为粗浅，墨子本不欲传下，但弟子们却喜其势简效宏，畅快淋漓，外出施技行侠，若遇怙恶不悛之辈，便以此术传道。历代门人更是勤修不辍，时时改良，甚至将鹰隼之力融入其中，使一门普通的拳法，变得有些——惊世骇俗！
en:
"I carry Heaven's Will, and by it, I make others yield."
The world believes Mohists favor the sword, yet few know they cherish the fist above all weapons. When Mozi founded his school, facing constant mockery, he reasoned with the reasonable and struck down the foolish. From this, a crude fist art emerged.
Though Mozi never meant to pass it down, disciples loved its simple power and used it to "enlighten" evildoers. Over generations, they refined it ceaselessly, even weaving in the striking force of hawks and falcons, transforming an ordinary style into something truly extraordinary.
