他感觉胸口一痛，温热的液体从心头直直喷洒，眼前一片猩红。
正好，看不见那小崽子的表情。
他不擅长看被留下之人的神情，叫人——觉得肉麻。

他也没想太多。只是觉得，那个毛都还没长齐的小崽子，还没见过江湖呢。
en:
Yi ao had always known that roaming the jianghu together would one day end. He had grown adept at this. 
He had grown adept at this. 
Yet he never expected the day to come so swiftly. 
When he threw the brat out, his heart felt calm and unburdened. The next instant, the demoness drew her blade and struck. 
A sharp pain seared through his chest, warm liquid spurting from his heart, painting his vision scarlet. 
Perfect—now he wouldn't have to see the brat's face. 
He'd never been good at reading the expressions of those left behind. They made him... uncomfortable.
 
He didn't think too deeply. Only that this barely fledged brat—hardly more than a child—had yet to truly see the jianghu.

zh: 《战国策》中记载：“民之所食，大抵豆饭藿羹。”黄豆在当时称为菽，是中国的最原生的物种，已经成为人们日常生活中的主食。而豆腐二字的首次出现却要晚上许多，到北宋时候才出现在由陶谷撰写的《清异录》中：“时戢为青阳丞，洁己勤民，肉味不给，日市豆腐数个，邑人呼豆腐为‘小宰羊‘。“因此学者们认为，豆腐可能在唐朝的时候才传到了中原，当唐末、五代的时候，才普遍成了老百姓的食物。
en: "Strategies of the Warring States" records: "What the people eat consists largely of bean meals and leaf soup." Soybeans, then called shu, were a native Chinese staple. However, the term "tofu" (doufu) appeared much later, first seen in the Northern Song text "Records of Strange Things" by Tao Gu: "Shi Ji, serving as an official in Qingyang, was honest and diligent. Lacking meat, he bought several pieces of tofu daily. The locals called tofu 'the little lamb'." Thus, scholars believe tofu likely spread to the Central Plains during the Tang Dynasty, becoming a common folk food by the late Tang and Five Dynasties period.

zh:
清泉驿的铜铃在风里响了二十年，刘三杨“诶诶”的应门声也及时了二十年，来自长安的花的肥的高的矮的各色驿马被他牵进来照顾了二十年，太阳出了二十年。
清泉驿里自豪又辛勤的驿夫们不记得他除了“老刘头”之外的名字和模样，仿佛他一出生就是个窝窝囊囊嘟嘟哝哝的老杂役。
老刘头作为清泉驿唯一一个并非驿夫，也不是兵卒出身，不用出门上路的普通人，最大的本事是让自己消失。
他总能在大家晚上聚在一起吃饭聊天，驿夫们一边大笑着喊“一驿过一驿，驿骑如流星”一边搂着人灌酒，高声自夸这一路见闻和惊险的时候，找到一个最不起眼的位置，让阴影恰到好处遮住佝偻的背。陈忠拉响清泉驿的铜铃，进门来宣布自己是新任命的驿长的那天，这个像一粒沙子般平凡的老头啃着胡饼，一如既往地给拉铃的人开了门。 
老刘头很满意自己日复一日的活计。马是不变的，铜铃是不变的，沙子是不变的。成为沙漠里一粒不起眼的沙子让他安心，日子像日头一样一成不变也让他安心。
但陈哥，就是陈忠，总不想叫他安心。陈忠不仅是个好人，还是个退下来的安西军老兵。人的腰咋能挺那么直呢，风要吹折的。刀也吓人，刀要见血的。还有陈哥嘴里念叨着的什么志向，什么心劲儿，都跟他那刀一样危险。别人眼里看不见他，但陈忠能看见他，他那让自己消失的本事在陈忠这儿不顶事了。
这个严肃的老兵总能把他从阴影中抓出来，给他带饭菜，教他拿刀，教他学武，问他将来想做点什么。他知道陈哥是对他好，但他也知道自己哪块料都不是。他甚至不敢躲着陈哥。 
他怕陈忠害了他。陈忠果然害了他。 
后来，铜铃声稀疏了，要他照顾的马也少了。夜晚的聚会，聚会上的驿夫，驿夫口袋里的口粮和铜钱，飘扬在夜空中的歌声和诗句都少了。老刘头木讷地重复着手里的活计。
他总觉着，头顶的日头也少了。但他只是一粒沙，估摸着要粘在谁的鞋底被带走吧。 
有一日，门口的铜铃又响了。他一如既往的去应门，一开门，日头便落了。 
年轻的唐兵拎着一口沉甸甸的麻布袋和滴着血的刀，怒目圆睁地站在门口，像一块等着粉身碎骨的石头。他还没来得及惊叫，风一吹，那唐兵就化在沙子里。 
他没敢听陈哥他们是怎么吵的架。他只知道，那天，清泉驿散了。最后留下的只有陈哥和一个不怕死的愣头青大锣子。
他是白丁，他不是兵，陈哥非说他是个兵，把他也算上凑满了一队，带着他上路了。他不想走，但是陈哥许诺他把这口麻布袋送回长安后就给他写调令，让他和麻布袋一起留在长安，不用再离开家乡了。 
回家。回家。回家…… 
回家的路难走。车丢了。马丢了。钱，口粮和水丢了。大锣子把命丢了。布袋里的种子丢的只剩小半袋。 
再后来，陈哥也丢了。 
没人再盯着他，叫他提起劲儿来了。他又可以消失了，像沙子消失在沙漠中。 
刘三杨迈了一步，踢到一口麻布袋。麻布袋孤零零站在天地之间，四面八方竟不知该往何处去。 
“你也没人要？” 
麻布做的袋子委屈地低着脑袋，委顿在沙地里。 
于是，他背起麻布袋。 
回家了。

人是沙漠里的一粒沙子，风一吹就跟着飘。 
但是当风往东边刮的时候，他会努力往上抬抬身子，好飘的更远些。
en:
For twenty years, the bronze bell of Qingquan Station had rung in the wind; for twenty years, Liu Sanyang's "Aye, aye" greeting at the door had been prompt; for twenty years, the variegated relay horses from Chang'an, spotted, plump, tall, short, had been led in and cared for by him; for twenty years, the sun had risen. 
The proud and diligent post riders of Qingquan Station didn't remember his name or face beyond Old Liu, it was as if he was born a grumbling, hapless old handyman. 
Old Liu, as the only person at Qingquan Station who wasn't a post rider, not of soldier stock, an ordinary man who didn't have to travel, his greatest skill was making himself disappear. 
He could always find the most inconspicuous spot when everyone gathered at night to eat and chat, when the post riders laughed and shouted "One station after another, the post horses like shooting stars!" while hugging people and forcing drinks, loudly boasting of their travels and dangers, letting the shadows perfectly cover his hunched back. The day Chen Zhong rang the bell of Qingquan Station and entered to announce he was the newly appointed station master, this old man, ordinary as a grain of sand, gnawing on a pancake, opened the door for the bell-ringer as usual.  
Old Liu was content with his day-in, day-out work. The horses were constant, the bronze bell was constant, the sand was constant. Being an inconspicuous grain of sand in the desert put him at ease, days unchanging like the sun put him at ease. 
But Brother Chen, that is, Chen Zhong, never wanted him at ease. Chen Zhong wasn't just a good man, he was a retired veteran of the Anxi Army. How could a man's back be so straight? The wind would break it. His sword was frightening too, a sword needed to see blood. And the aspirations, the drive that Brother Chen muttered about, they were as dangerous as his sword. Others couldn't see him, but Chen Zhong could see him. His skill of disappearing didn't work with Chen Zhong. 
This serious old soldier would always pull him from the shadows, bring him food, teach him to hold a sword, teach him martial arts, ask him what he wanted to do in the future. He knew Brother Chen meant well, but he also knew he wasn't cut out for anything. He didn't even dare hide from Brother Chen.  
He feared Chen Zhong would ruin him. And Chen Zhong did ruin him.  
Later, the bell rang less often, and the horses needing his care dwindled. The nightly gatherings, the post riders at the gatherings, the rations and copper coins in their pockets, the songs and poems floating in the night sky, all grew fewer. Old Liu numbly repeated his tasks. 
He always felt the sun overhead was also less. But he was just a grain of sand, destined to stick to someone's sole and be carried away.  
One day, the bronze bell at the door rang again. He went to answer as usual, and upon opening the door, the sun set.  
A young Tang soldier stood at the door, holding a heavy hemp sack and a dripping, bloody sword, eyes wide with fury, like a rock waiting to be shattered. Before he could scream, a gust of wind blew, and the Tang soldier dissolved into the sand.  
He didn't dare listen to how Brother Chen and the others argued. He only knew that day, Qingquan Station disbanded. In the end, only Brother Chen and a reckless young tough called Da Luozi remained. 
He was a commoner, not a soldier, but Brother Chen insisted he was a soldier, counted him to fill out a squad, and took him on the road. He didn't want to go, but Brother Chen promised to write him a transfer order after delivering this Burlap Sack to Chang'an, letting him stay in Chang'an with the sack, never having to leave home again.  
Go home. Go home. Go home...  
The road home was hard. The cart was lost. The horses were lost. Money, rations, and water were lost. Da Luozi lost his life. The seeds in the sack were lost until only less than half remained.  
Later still, Brother Chen was lost too.  
No one watched him anymore, urged him to gather strength. He could disappear again, like sand vanishing in the desert.  
Liu Sanyang took a step and kicked a Burlap Sack. The sack stood alone between heaven and earth, with no direction to go in all four quarters.  
"No one wants you either?"  
The sack, made of burlap, lowered its head in grievance, sagging in the sand.  
So, he shouldered the burlap sack.  
He was going home. 

A person is a grain of sand in the desert, blowing wherever the wind goes.  
But when the wind blows east, he'll strive to lift himself a bit higher, to float a little farther.
